title: Book Fifteen opens: come before God clean and washed
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK FIFTEEN. That we must stand before God clean and washed, and that our cleansing, once again, is in Christ.
Cyril: From the whole of our discussion, Palladius, a clear and evident proof has been gathered for us that we must go…
translator_notes: PG 68.949. The section is the book heading, its argument line, and the first words of Cyril's opening sentence; the column cut falls after ἰέναι and the sentence continues in §2 (παγκάλως εἰς οἶκον Θεοῦ). Ἐκ παντὸς λόγου taken as 'from the whole of our discussion' (the preceding books), not 'from every word'. No Scripture in this section; Isaiah 66:2 follows in §2.

title: We all stumble, so God sent his Son to cleanse us
english: Cyril: …into the house of God in the finest way, shining and washed, and winning close fellowship with him through sanctification. For then we shall find God gracious, and, if we may put it so, looking on our affairs with his whole eye and showing the saints the sparing care that best befits them. ‘On whom shall I look,’ he says, ‘but on the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words?’ (Isaiah 66:2) For the one who is in this state will truly lift up holy hands (1 Timothy 2:8), and his cry will reach the very ear of the Godhead, so that, once he has obtained whatever he may pray for, he can even say in his great joy: ‘He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears.’ (Psalm 18:6) Or have you not plainly learned this from the inspired David, who sings to us that ‘the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer’? (Psalm 34:15)
Palladius: I have learned it.

Cyril: That this saying is true, no one may rightly doubt. But as for the need to wipe away our defilements, what way of doing it could there be for us? For no one will discern his transgressions (Psalm 19:12), and we all stumble in many ways (James 3:2). Our nature is sick with a proneness to sin, and it is very easily goaded into a settled bent for wrongdoing, since our inclination toward what is base smooths for us, in a way, the road of monstrous and loathsome pleasure.
Palladius: You are right. I would agree without a moment's delay with one who has chosen to speak correctly.

Cyril: For the flesh that comes from the earth has already fallen sick with the law of sin within it (Romans 7:23), and the human mind is very easily led astray, so that it turns aside toward evil from youth, as it is written (Genesis 8:21). That is why the sacred word rightly grieves over us: ‘For all,’ it says, ‘have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, not even one.’ (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:12) But since there was no turning away from evil, God the Father sent us his own Son from heaven as Savior and Redeemer, to justify by faith and set free from punishment, to make the feeble very strong, to enlighten what was darkened, to turn back what was wandering, and to draw out from the devil's greed what lay prostrate beneath him.

Palladius: So it is in Christ that we shall scrub away the shame that comes from sin; and once scoured clean in this way, and keeping as far as possible from every blemish, we shall approach God the Father through him.

Cyril: You understand it very well. One may hear the holy prophets themselves proclaiming aloud this grace, so worthy of our wonder and so long prayed for. Micah, most wise, says something like this: ‘Who is a God like you, taking away iniquities and passing over unrighteous deeds for the remnant of his inheritance? And he did not hold his anger as a witness, for he delights in mercy.’ (Micah 7:18) And another says again: ‘Remember these things, Jacob and Israel; do not forget me. For behold, I have wiped away your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a thick darkness.’ (Isaiah 44:21–22) And one could gather a great many more such passages…
translator_notes: PG 68.949. Opens mid-sentence from §1 (ἰέναι παγκάλως). LXX Psalm renumbering: LXX Ps 17:7 = English Psalm 18:6 (same words also in 2 Samuel 22:7; cited to the Psalm because Cyril's phrase 'from his holy temple' matches both, and the following David quotation shows he is reading the Psalter); LXX Ps 33:16 = English Psalm 34:15; LXX Ps 18:13 = English Psalm 19:12 (Cyril turns the Psalm's question 'Who will discern transgressions?' into a statement 'no one will discern'); LXX Ps 13:3 = English Psalm 14:3, quoted in the same words in Romans 3:12, so both cited. 'Lift up holy hands' (ὁσίας ἀνατενεῖ χεῖρας) echoes 1 Timothy 2:8 (ἐπαίροντας ὁσίους χεῖρας); cited as a clear allusion. 'Law of sin' in the flesh = Romans 7:23. 'Toward evil from youth, as it is written' = Genesis 8:21 LXX (ἐπὶ τὰ πονηρὰ ἐκ νεότητος). 'We all stumble in many ways' = James 3:2 nearly verbatim. Micah 7:18 follows the LXX ('did not hold his anger as a witness', εἰς μαρτύριον, where the Hebrew has 'for ever'). Isaiah 44:21-22 LXX: the OCR has ὡς ἐν νεφέλῃ ... ὡς γνόφος where the LXX reads ὡς νεφέλην ... ὡς γνόφον; the sense is the same. Uncited possible allusions: the Father sending the Son as Savior (1 John 4:14); justifying by faith (Romans 3:28-30). Doubtful reading: εὐπάροιστος is unusual and may be an OCR or print form (perhaps from παροιστράω, 'goad to frenzy'); rendered 'easily goaded' and flagged. φειδώ rendered 'tender forbearance' (sparing care). Palladius' reply Ἐπυθόμην carries a stray question mark in the source; read as a statement. Section ends mid-sentence (τὰ | ἀπὸ τῆς θείας Γραφῆς) and continues in §3.

title: Two kinds of sacrifice, and the rule against blemish
english: Cyril: …from the divine Scripture, showing very well what is true for us in these matters; but to heap up still more where the proof is already clear and evident is, I think, superfluous.
Palladius: That the matter is evident is plain to everyone. But for my part I would like to see the cleansing in Christ in the images of the law as well.

Cyril: Look, then, if you wish, and if it seems good that we go this way. The law ordered those who were defiled, and those who had fallen under charges of transgression, to offer sacrifice, and it divided the kinds of sacrifice in two. Some portray Emmanuel slain on our behalf; others portray us ourselves, dying to the world and offering up to God our own life and salvation as a fragrant aroma. For is it not by putting to death our members that are on earth (Colossians 3:5), and freeing the mind from worldly distraction and from earthier pleasures, that we shall live out the divine life of the Gospel?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: The sacrifice, then, is the spiritual cleansing that comes, as it were, through the death of Christ; while the vow and the gift, on our side, is to dedicate to God a life well ordered and lived in holiness. Yet the law lays it down beforehand and clearly and solemnly testifies that the offerings made in these matters must be without blemish, and this is both useful and necessary. Since some of the victims offered showed Christ as slain for us, while others represent us, all but burning our own life as incense to God, for this very reason the law says that they must be without blemish and in no way afflicted with any defect. For Christ is without blemish, since he committed no sin (1 Peter 2:22); and God would not accept us either while we are still in our defilements and sick with the misery of sin. So it is written in Leviticus (Leviticus 22:17–23): ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, and to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, and you shall say to them: Any man of the sons of Israel, or of the proselytes attached to them in Israel, who offers his gifts for any of their vows or any of their freewill offerings, whatever they offer to God as a whole burnt offering, what is acceptable for you is a male without blemish from the herds, from the sheep, and from the goats. Whatever has a blemish in it they shall not bring to the Lord, for it will not be acceptable for you. And whoever offers a sacrifice of salvation to the Lord, fulfilling a vow, or as a freewill offering, or at your feasts, from the herds or from the sheep, it shall be without blemish to be accepted; there shall be no blemish in it. Blind, or broken, or with its tongue cut, or with warts, or with festering mange, or with scabs: they shall not bring these to God, and you shall not give any of them as a burnt offering on the altar to the Lord. And a calf or a sheep with cropped ears…
translator_notes: PG 68.952. Opens mid-sentence from §2. πίστις in the first sentence is taken as 'proof' (assurance), not religious faith, because it pairs with ἀπόδειξις in §1 and the point is that the case is already proven. The Leviticus quotation is LXX Leviticus 22:17-23a and runs on into §4 (22:23b-25); the inline citation is placed at Cyril's introduction because the quotation is cut by the column break. LXX terms kept: ὁμολογία = vow, αἵρεσις = freewill offering, θυσία σωτηρίου = 'sacrifice of salvation' (the LXX name for the peace offering; kept literal because Cyril reads salvation typology in these offerings), κάρπωσις = burnt offering. γλωσσότμητος ('with its tongue cut') is the LXX rendering where the Hebrew has 'maimed'; Cyril builds on the LXX word later. 'Without blemish' (ἄμωμος) kept consistently because Cyril's argument turns on it. Uncited possible allusions: 'dying to the world' (Galatians 6:14; Colossians 2:20), 'a fragrant aroma' (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας, a stock Levitical phrase, also Ephesians 5:2). 'He committed no sin' = 1 Peter 2:22 (from Isaiah 53:9).

title: The unblemished male as a type of Christ and of us
english: Cyril: …or a docked tail, you may slaughter them for yourself, but for your vow it will not be accepted. An animal that is bruised or crushed, gelded or torn, you shall not bring to the Lord, and you shall not do this in your land. And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer the gifts of your God from any of these, because there is corruption in them and a blemish in them. They will not be accepted for you.’ (Leviticus 22:23–25) Notice, then, that the law plainly and openly charges both those of Israel's blood and those from outside who have been admitted into the people, I mean the proselytes, that they must inspect the sacred offerings carefully for blemishes. For it said that what we bring must be male and without blemish, that is, strong and above the passions. For softness, an effeminate cast of mind, and also being sick with an inward defect, a maiming of the mind, are wholly unacceptable to God and rejected. Or would you not say that anyone in whom these things are seen is unholy?
Palladius: How could I not?

Cyril: So what is feeble and, as it were, slack is rejected, while what is strong, as pictured in the nature of males, is accepted, if it also has blamelessness joined to it. Such things would serve us as a clear type of Christ. For Emmanuel is at once male and without blemish, since he is truly the power of God (1 Corinthians 1:24) and knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). He is male in another sense too: for the male always stands first and holds the higher place over the other, and besides this it is the one most fitted to lead. And the Son stands at the head, holds a place incomparably higher, and leads the universe, even though he became like us, and the Shepherd was, for our good, counted among the sheep. But among the victims, those that are unholy and to be sent away are the blind, the broken, and also the one with its tongue cut, the one with warts, with festering mange, with scabs, with cropped ears, or with a docked tail. And the same holds, it says, if any animal's male parts should happen to be crushed, and so it should bear the forced condition that already places it among eunuchs. For this, I think, is what ‘bruised and crushed, gelded and torn’ means.
Palladius: Should we, then, apply these things to our own character and ways of life?

Cyril: Certainly. For in no other way than this would the law be spiritual for us (Romans 7:14). God would set no store by a worship carried on as in shadows, nor would he ever have laid down its laws, if he were not sketching in it beforehand the surpassing beauty of the truth.
Palladius: Well said. Then go through the meaning of each one, and explain again what it would be.

Cyril: I will go on, then, and very gladly. ‘Blind’ seems to mean the one without wisdom and understanding, who has no divine light in himself, that is, the enlightenment that comes through Christ in the Spirit; and the one who is senseless and still without faith is wholly unholy. ‘For if you do not believe,’ it says, ‘you will not understand.’ (Isaiah 7:9) ‘Broken’…
translator_notes: PG 68.953. Opens mid-quotation (LXX Leviticus 22:23b-25), continued from §3. LXX σφάγια ποιήσεις αὐτὰ σεαυτῷ rendered 'you may slaughter for yourself' (for ordinary use, not as a vowed offering). θλαδίαν καὶ ἐκτεθλιμμένον καὶ ἐκτομίαν καὶ ἀπεσπασμένον = animals with damaged or removed testicles; rendered 'bruised or crushed, gelded or torn', which Cyril himself then explains as damage to the male parts. The OCR punctuation φρόνημα· τὸ θηλυπρεπές is read as one phrase, 'an effeminate cast of mind' (stray raised dot). Cyril's statements about the male 'standing first' and 'most fitted to lead' reflect ancient assumptions and are translated as written, without softening. 'The power of God' = 1 Corinthians 1:24 (Χριστὸν Θεοῦ δύναμιν); 'knew no sin' = 2 Corinthians 5:21 (τὸν μὴ γνόντα ἁμαρτίαν). 'The law is spiritual' = Romans 7:14. Isaiah 7:9 is quoted in the LXX form ('you will not understand'); the Hebrew reads 'you will not be established'. Uncited possible allusions: 'the Shepherd counted among the sheep' may adapt Isaiah 53:12 ('He was counted among the lawless') and the shepherd of John 10:11, but the wording is Cyril's own; 'worship as in shadows' recalls Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1 without quoting them. Section ends inside a word (Συντετριμμέ|νον), continuing in §5; the English stops at 'Broken'.

title: Blemished offerings as sicknesses of the soul
english: Cyril: …in turn, seems to mean the person who is sick in every way and has nothing at all sound in him, who cannot walk straight, that is, has no strength to do anything good, and falls wholly short of the strength that is in Christ and in the Spirit. Something like this has happened to those of whom it is written through one of the holy prophets: ‘Thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing weakness upon this people, and fathers and sons together shall grow weak in it; the neighbor and his friend shall perish’ (Jeremiah 6:21). But our divine Psalmist presents those who have been justified by faith in Christ as joyful, singing psalms and saying: ‘Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption’ (Psalm 103:2–4). The animal with a cut tongue, as I think, is the one who does not know how to speak rightly and has no strength to proclaim, as it is written, ‘the word of faith which we preach’ (Romans 10:8), ‘the appeal to God from a good conscience’ (1 Peter 3:21). Yet the prophet will make plain that at the coming of Christ they will throw off this kind of disease too, when he says: ‘And the stammering tongues will quickly learn to speak peace’ (Isaiah 32:4). So the one with a cut tongue is the one who still stammers and has not yet been taught to speak the peace that comes to us from above and from the Father, that is, Christ (Ephesians 2:14), or the things concerning him. The animals with warts, with festering mange, or with scabs (Leviticus 22:22) we take to be those who have within themselves a mind in the grip of passion and are deeply sick with the corruption that lies in sin, yet never consider that they ought to reduce them, but rather let them creep on toward what is more shameful and spread toward what is worse. For warts and festering mange and scabs plainly always grow, tend somehow toward a worse state, and little by little spread over the whole body. So too are the passions in our souls that are not cut short but always race on toward the worse, as if with a rush that nothing holds back. The animal with its ears cut off, and besides it the one with a docked tail (Leviticus 22:23), would signify the person who is hard to persuade and will not listen, and the one who is not seemly in every respect. Or is the harm not to the hearing, for those whose ear has been cut off?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: And animals that have no tail, would you yourself grant that they have the finest form? Not at all; for in themselves they are badly marred by unsightliness. So the person hinted at indirectly, as it were by an animal that has no tail, is unseemly and lacks beauty. The law also rejects what is male by nature but cannot do what males do; I mean the bruised and the cut (Leviticus 22:24). Such again would be those who have a reputation for the manly courage that leads to virtue, yet are not actually active in pursuit of the glories of virtue; they are dry, as it were, and barren, and in many ways robbed of the power to bear fruit. For a vast crowd of unholy passions forces us into weakness and impotence, and besides this into being unable to bear fruit. This is why, I think, the law calls by many names…
translator_notes: Boundary: the Greek word Συντετριμμένον is split across sections 4 and 5 (Συντετριμμέ | νον). Section 4's English ends with ‘Broken’…, so section 5 opens '…in turn, seems to mean' without repeating the word; ἔοικε ... λέγειν from section 4 governs the clause (same 'seems to mean' as 'Blind' in section 4). The section ends mid-sentence: πολλοῖς ὀνόμασι τὸ | εὐνουχισθὲν ὁ νόμος ἀποκαλεῖ, finished in section 6. LXX: Psalm 102:2–4 LXX = Psalm 103:2–4 English; Cyril omits 'who forgives all your iniquities' (v. 3a). Jeremiah 6:21 follows the LXX ('weakness', ἀσθένεια) where the Hebrew has 'stumbling blocks'. Isaiah 32:4 follows the LXX ('speak peace'). 'The word of faith which we preach' is Romans 10:8; 'appeal to God from a good conscience' is 1 Peter 3:21 (Cyril joins them with 'as it is written'). 'The peace ... that is, Christ' cited to Ephesians 2:14 ('He himself is our peace') as a clear allusion. Levitical blemish terms come from Leviticus 22:22–24 LXX, quoted in section 4; cited here where each term group is interpreted. μυρμηκιῶν = with warts; ψωραγριῶν = with wild (festering) mange; λειχῆνας ἔχον = with lichen-like eruptions, rendered 'scabs'. ὀρθοποδεῖν ('walk straight') echoes Galatians 2:14 only in vocabulary: not cited. Doubtful: αὐτοὺς in οὐ μὴν ὅτι χρὴ καὶ πρὸς τὸ μεῖον ἄγειν αὐτούς is masculine plural; taken as the skin conditions just named (λειχῆνας is the nearest masculine noun), rendered 'them' to keep the Greek's ambiguity; it could also be reflexive ('bring themselves down'). Possible allusion, uncited: 'spread little by little over the whole body' may echo 2 Timothy 2:17 (spreading like gangrene). Μελῳδός ('Singer') rendered 'Psalmist' (David).

title: Access to the Father through Christ alone; leaven and honey
english: Cyril: …the animal that has been gelded. For it says ‘bruised and crushed, cut and torn’ (Leviticus 22:24); for the passions in us are of every kind, and lead us, as it were, by a long road into weakness and impotence.
Palladius: The argument is convincing.

Cyril: Besides these things the law further declared that it is abominable to offer sacrifices to God through a foreign hand as well, saying: ‘And from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer the gifts to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 22:25). By this it is signified in type that the Father can be approached through Christ alone. For he is our truly unblemished and great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), the Mediator in the divine economy (1 Timothy 2:5). For as the inspired Paul writes: ‘In him we have gained access in the Spirit to the Father’ (Ephesians 2:18). So those who choose to consecrate their own souls to God the Father, with Christ as Mediator, ought to be free of blemish. ‘For you shall be holy,’ he says, ‘as I am holy’ (Leviticus 11:44).
Palladius: You have spoken excellently.

Cyril: Having set in order the ways of sacrifice as they concern cattle and sheep, the law comes to us through other figures as well, and urges most earnestly that those who are accustomed to do this must approach God without blame. For it says again in Leviticus: ‘Every sacrifice that you offer to the Lord, you shall not offer leavened. For you shall not offer any leaven or any honey from it to make a burnt offering to the Lord. You shall offer them to the Lord as a gift of firstfruits, but they shall not be brought up onto the altar for a fragrant aroma to the Lord. And every gift of your sacrifice shall be salted with salt. You shall not leave the salt of the covenant to the Lord out of your sacrifices; with every gift of yours you shall offer salt to the Lord your God’ (Leviticus 2:11–13). Leaven, then, would be a type of shrewdness, and not by any means only of the kind that is blamed, but of the other kind too, I mean the good kind that is praised, which the word of Wisdom also promises to give to the innocent (Proverbs 1:4). For the word ‘shrewdness’ is, in a sense, neutral. Honey, in turn, sometimes hints to us indirectly at bodily pleasure, as in the saying: ‘Do not give heed to a worthless woman; for honey drips from the lips of a prostitute’ (Proverbs 5:3). But at other times it gives a picture of good sweetness. For it is written: ‘Eat honey, my son, for the honeycomb is good, that your throat may be sweetened’ (Proverbs 24:13). So the law forbids that leaven and honey be brought for a burnt offering and sacrifice. It accepts them from the one who brings them as a gift and as firstfruits, but by no means carries them up for a fragrant aroma to God.
Palladius: Then explain, in turn, what the riddle means.
Cyril: The matter is hard to grasp, Palladius. For what it might mean that these things are by no means rejected, and yet are not carried up as a burnt offering and a sacrifice…

A stray closing guillemet (») after ἀδρανές in the source closes no quotation; ignored. Boundary out: section 6 ends inside the word θυ|σίαν; the sentence continues in section 7 with ἀνακομίζειν αὐτά, πῶς οὐκ ἄναντες ἰδεῖν. For English word order the verb 'carried up' (ἀνακομίζειν) is rendered at the end of section 6, and section 7 opens with the main clause 'how could anyone not find that steep…'. 'Great High Priest' cited to Hebrews 4:14; 'unblemished' may also echo Hebrews 9:14 and 7:26 (not cited separately). 'Mediator' cited to 1 Timothy 2:5. οἰκονομικῶς rendered 'in the divine economy' (the incarnate dispensation). Ephesians 2:18 is quoted loosely ('in Him' for 'through Him'; Ephesians 3:12 is close too). 'You shall be holy as I am holy' cited to Leviticus 11:44; the same words occur at Leviticus 19:2, 20:26 and 1 Peter 1:16 (καθώς is nearer 1 Peter 1:15–16). Leviticus 2:11–13 LXX: Cyril reads οὐ προσοίσετε ζυμωτήν (Rahlfs οὐ ποιήσετε ζυμωτόν) and ἅλας διαθήκης Κυρίῳ (Rahlfs κυρίου); rendered as Cyril has it. Proverbs 1:4 LXX 'to give shrewdness (πανουργίαν) to the innocent' is the 'word of Wisdom'. Proverbs 5:3 cites the LXX form, which adds 'Do not give heed to a worthless woman'. Proverbs 24:13 numbering is the same in LXX (Rahlfs) and English. πανουργία rendered 'shrewdness' throughout (neutral sense, as Cyril says it is a 'middle' word). κάρπωμα / καρπῶσαι rendered 'burnt offering'.

title: Shrewdness, marriage and salt
english: Cyril: …how could it not be uphill work to see? I think, then, that even the shrewd conduct a holy and good soul sometimes shows, if it is practiced at the right time and has piety toward God as its motive, is not rejected by him; yet it will not be ranked on an equal footing with fragrant virtue, nor would it be counted as a spiritual sacrifice. For simplicity is more precious with God. For Holy Scripture admires the inspired Jacob, saying: ‘And Jacob was a guileless man, living in a house’ (Genesis 25:27). For shrewdness is far removed from all who are innocent. And to the holy apostles the Savior himself said: ‘Be wise as serpents and innocent as doves’ (Matthew 10:16). Yet innocence is precious with God, and compared with the other is in every way the better. But shrewd and wily conduct is fitting for the management of the apostolic mission; the blessed Paul too made use of it at times, everywhere escaping an untimely death at the hands of his enemies. So shrewdness, in godly pursuits, might well be acceptable, but it would by no means be counted as the fragrance of virtue if it were tested by its own nature. In the same way honey too, taken as a type of fleshly pleasure, would point, I think, to this life in the world, which is not free of the pleasures of the flesh. For marriage is honorable (Hebrews 13:4), serving the bearing of children, and blameless according to the law when it is lived in Christ. Yet this will not count for anyone as the strength of virtue, nor will it be ranked equal with the glories of self-control. And the blessed Paul too writes to the married: ‘Do not separate from one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, so that you may give yourselves to prayer and supplication’ (1 Corinthians 7:5). And again: ‘Be together,’ he says, ‘so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control’ (1 Corinthians 7:5). And he added to this: ‘I say this by way of concession, not of command’ (1 Corinthians 7:6). Do you see, then, that he grants a concession to the married? How then can something that is met with a concession be a virtue? ‘Concerning the virgin,’ he says (1 Corinthians 7:25), ‘she is more blessed if she remains as she is’ (1 Corinthians 7:40), that is, unmarried. So honey is not rejected, for marriage is acceptable; yet it is not offered for a fragrant aroma, as the ways of virtue are. But salt is also sprinkled on the sacrifices; for I think we must offer sacrifice wisely and with understanding, and be well seasoned for every good thing. For what is graceless and tasteless would least of all befit those who have chosen to live devoutly. This is why the Savior said to the holy disciples: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew 5:13). And Paul too writes: ‘Let your speech be seasoned with grace and salt (Colossians 4:6), that it may give grace to those who hear’ (Ephesians 4:29).
Palladius: It is settled, then, that good sense and graciousness are signified by the salt.
Cyril: So it is. And now, I think, having carefully marked out the ways in which one must offer sacrifice, we must next observe from the sacred Scriptures themselves…
translator_notes: Boundary in: section 7 opens inside θυ|σίαν ἀνακομίζειν αὐτά, πῶς οὐκ ἄναντες ἰδεῖν; 'sacrifice' and 'carried up' are rendered at the end of section 6, so section 7 opens with the main clause. ἄναντες ('uphill') rendered 'uphill work'. Boundary out: section 7 ends with the article τό; the clause continues in section 8 (ὅπως ἂν γένοιτο ... 'how those sick with sin may escape the disease'). The English ends '…we must next observe from the sacred Scriptures themselves…', and section 8 begins with 'how'. Scripture: Genesis 25:27 LXX (ἄπλαστος, 'plain, guileless'; English Bibles 'a quiet/plain man'). 1 Corinthians 7:5 is quoted loosely ('do not separate', Greek NT 'do not deprive'); both halves of the verse are cited at 7:5. 'Concerning the virgin ... more blessed if she remains so' joins 1 Corinthians 7:25 (opening words, Greek NT plural 'virgins') with 7:40 (said there of the widow); cited to both. Hebrews 13:4 ('marriage is honorable') is a clear allusion. 'Seasoned with grace and salt' is Colossians 4:6 ('with grace, seasoned with salt'); 'that it may give grace to those who hear' is Ephesians 4:29; Cyril joins them as one quotation. Doubtful readings: πονηρόν in τὸ πανοῦργον καὶ πονηρόν literally means 'bad, wicked'; here it seems to mean 'sly' and is rendered 'wily'; possibly a corrupt reading. καθ' ἕτερόν που πάντων ἐν ἀμείνοσιν rendered 'compared with the other is in every way the better'; it could also mean 'in another respect ranks among the best of all'. διηρτημένους (from διαρτάω, 'separated, hung') makes little sense; read as διηρτυμένους ('seasoned', cf. ἠρτυμένος in Colossians 4:6) and rendered 'well seasoned'. Uncited possible allusions: Paul's escapes (2 Corinthians 11:32–33; Acts 9:25) and Paul calling himself 'crafty' (πανοῦργος, 2 Corinthians 12:16); 'spiritual sacrifice' (θυσία νοητή) may echo Romans 12:1 or 1 Peter 2:5; 'fragrance of virtue' may echo 2 Corinthians 2:15 or Ephesians 5:2.

title: The sin offering of a calf for the priest and the people
english: Cyril: …how those who have fallen sick with sin may escape the disease and ward off the harm that comes from transgression. Now it is written in Leviticus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: If a soul sins unintentionally before the Lord against any of the commandments of the Lord, in things that ought not to be done, and does any one of them: if the anointed high priest sins so as to make the people sin, he shall bring for the sin that he has committed a calf from the herd, without blemish, to the Lord for the sin. He shall bring the calf to the door of the tent of witness before the Lord, lay his hand on the head of the calf before the Lord, and slaughter the calf before the Lord. And the anointed priest, whose hands have been consecrated, shall take some of the blood of the calf and bring it into the tent of witness; and the priest shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times before the Lord, in front of the holy veil. And the priest shall put some of the blood of the calf on the horns of the altar of compounded incense that is before the Lord, which is in the tent of witness. And all the blood of the calf he shall pour out at the base of the altar of whole burnt offerings, which is by the doors of the tent of witness. And all the fat of the calf of the sin offering he shall take from it: the fat that covers the entrails, and all the fat on the entrails, and the two kidneys and the fat on them, which is on the thighs, and the lobe of the liver; he shall remove it with the kidneys, just as it is removed from the calf of the peace offering, and the priest shall offer it up on the altar of burnt offering. As for the skin of the calf and all its flesh, with the head, the extremities, the belly and the dung, they shall carry the whole calf outside the camp to a clean place where they pour out the ashes, and they shall burn it on wood with fire; it shall be burned where the ashes are poured out’ (Leviticus 4:1–12). This, then, is what he says about a ruler who leads the peoples under his hand to fall short of what is right along with him. And at once he declared further: ‘If the whole congregation of the sons of Israel errs through ignorance, and a matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation, and they do, against any of the commandments of the Lord, one thing that ought not to be done, and they transgress, and the sin that they committed in it becomes known to them, then the congregation shall bring a calf from the herd, without blemish, for the sin’ (Leviticus 4:13–14). And he states plainly that it must be offered in the same manner as the first.
Palladius: And what, again, is the meaning of these passages?

Cyril: It is clear, Palladius, and not hard to grasp, at least for anyone of sound mind. For in Christ is the cleansing of priests and of people, of small and great, in short of all, even if one by one we should happen to be caught transgressing, through not knowing the divine law…
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: section 7 ends with the article τό, which governs the clause ‘how those who have fallen sick…’; the English marks the break with an ellipsis. Section ends mid-sentence before ἤγουν, which opens section 9; English marks the break with an ellipsis. The Leviticus 4:1–12 quotation follows the LXX: ‘the anointed priest, whose hands have been consecrated’ renders ὁ χριστὸς ὁ τετελειωμένος τὰς χεῖρας (LXX idiom for ordination); ‘on the thighs’ renders LXX μηρίων (Hebrew: loins); θυσία τοῦ σωτηρίου is rendered ‘peace offering’ (lit. ‘sacrifice of salvation/deliverance’); θυσιαστήριον τῆς καρπώσεως is rendered ‘altar of burnt offering’. In 4:11–12 the skin and flesh are grammatically taken up by ‘they shall carry the whole calf’, so the English uses ‘As for…’. Cyril calls the anointed high priest of 4:3 an ἄρχων (‘ruler’) in his comment, and συναφαμαρτεῖν αὐτῷ τοῦ πρέποντος is taken as ‘to fall short of what is right along with him’ (ἀφαμαρτάνω + genitive). ἀκουσίως is rendered ‘unintentionally’ in the Leviticus quotations. ‘Small and great’ may echo Psalm 115:13 (LXX 113:21) but is too general to cite. μόσχος is rendered ‘calf’ in the quotation as in Cyril’s comments (sections 9–10), so the type reads consistently; ‘does one of all the commandments … that ought not to be done’ recast as ‘does, against any of the commandments of the Lord, one thing that ought not to be done’; εὖ μάλα φησί is an intensifier (‘states plainly’), not praise.

title: Christ the slain calf, and the place outside the gate
english: Cyril: …or through being forced, perhaps against our will, into what least pleases God, the Master of all. That is why the divine David also cried out for us: ‘Do not remember the sins of my youth and of my ignorance’ (Psalm 25:7). And since God is good by nature, kind and compassionate, and well aware of the weakness of our nature, the blessed Job all but openly accuses him of delaying and holding back from forgiving people their sins. For he speaks thus: ‘And why did You not grant forgetfulness of my lawlessness and cleansing of my sin?’ (Job 7:21) So the law proclaims aloud as well that in Christ, and in him alone, those held fast by sins will be justified through faith. For he is the one slaughtered for us like a calf at the doors of the sacred and divine tent, to open wide for us the way inside; he himself takes away our sins, as the prophet’s voice says (Isaiah 53:4). For this, I think, is what the laying of hands on the calf signifies. He himself entered the Holy of Holies through blood and obtained a holy redemption for us (Hebrews 9:12), and by one offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14), as the blessed Paul says. He it is who sanctifies the Church by the sprinkling of his own blood, and does so abundantly. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall dip his finger in the blood and sprinkle some of the blood seven times with his finger before the Lord’ (Leviticus 4:6). ‘For we have come,’ it says, ‘to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and to the blood of sprinkling that speaks better than Abel’ (Hebrews 12:22–24). Abel’s blood cried out to God (Genesis 4:10), condemning the murderer; but the precious blood of Christ, the Savior of us all, speaks better things to God on our behalf, for it was poured out as the price given in exchange for the life of all. The blood of the calf was poured out at the base of the altar, for the death of Christ is truly holy and sacred. And the inward parts are offered up: the fat, the kidneys and the lobe of the liver. For everything in Christ is fragrant, both what is seen outwardly and what is hidden; for the Word was holy, and there was nothing in him that was not pure. But the skin and the rest are burned outside the gate, for the law does not leave even the place of his passion unmarked for us. That is why the divine Paul said to us: ‘Let us therefore go forth outside the gate, bearing his reproach’ (Hebrews 13:12–13), that is, the cross borne for us and because of us. And the Savior himself says somewhere: ‘Whoever does not take his cross and follow after Me is not worthy of Me’ (Matthew 10:38). The most holy Paul seems to understand ‘outside the gate’ as ‘outside the world’, for the will to follow Christ takes us out of worldly life. Paul will bear witness again, for he said this about Christ: ‘Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world’ (Galatians 6:14). And though the saints walk on the earth, they strive to live no longer in an earthly way, but rather to have their citizenship in heaven (Philippians 3:20).
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence (ἤγουν continues the clause begun at the end of section 8); English marks it with an ellipsis. The section ends on a word split across the column break, πολί|τευμα; the whole word ‘citizenship’ is rendered here, so section 10 begins with the next sentence. Psalm 25:7 is LXX Psalm 24:7 (wording matches the LXX exactly). Job 7:21 matches the LXX. ‘He himself takes away our sins, as the prophet’s voice says’: Cyril’s ὁ τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν αἴρων blends Isaiah 53:4 LXX (οὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει, ‘our sins’) with the participle of John 1:29 (ὁ αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου, spoken by the Baptist, whom Cyril could also call a prophet); Isaiah 53:4 is cited as the likelier source and John 1:29 is left uncited. Hebrews 9:12 has ‘eternal redemption’ (αἰωνίαν λύτρωσιν); Cyril reads ‘holy redemption’ (ἁγίαν), kept as he wrote it. Leviticus 4:6 LXX lacks the second ‘with his finger’ (τῷ δακτύλῳ), which Cyril adds; the parallel Leviticus 4:17 differs more (ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος, ῥανεῖ), so 4:6 is cited. ‘The Church of the firstborn’ renders ἐκκλησίᾳ πρωτοτόκων in Hebrews 12:23, kept as ‘Church’ because Cyril has just spoken of Christ sanctifying the Church. ‘Abel’s blood cried out to God’ alludes to Genesis 4:10 (φωνὴ αἵματος… βοᾷ πρός με) and is cited. Hebrews 13:13 reads ‘outside the camp’; Cyril’s ‘outside the gate’ comes from Hebrews 13:12, so the citation covers 13:12–13. Leviticus 4:12 itself says ‘outside the camp’; Cyril’s ‘outside the gate’ follows Hebrews. ἀπαράδεκτον (‘the law does not leave even the place of his passion…’) is a doubtful word here; it is taken as ‘not handed on, unshown’, i.e. the law signals even the place of the passion. The sanctifying ‘sprinkling of his own blood’ may echo Hebrews 13:12 or 1 Peter 1:2 but is not cited as doubtful. ‘Justified through faith in Christ alone’ may echo Galatians 2:16 or Romans 3:28 and ‘open wide for us the way inside’ may echo Hebrews 10:19–20; both left uncited as doubtful. ἀντάλλαγμα (‘price given in exchange’) is not cited. Philippians 3:20 (ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει) is a clear allusion and is cited. ἀπαράδεκτον is probably ἀπαράδεικτον (‘not pointed out’); rendered ‘does not leave … unmarked for us’.

title: Ash and water, and victims matched to the sin
english: Cyril: …And for those who have been defiled, the cleansing is the ash with water (Numbers 19:17). For the Savior’s passion is the ransom from sin; he sanctifies us through water, through which we gain not the removal of the filth of the flesh, as it is written (1 Peter 3:21), but the washing away of the defilements in our souls. For ‘Wash yourselves,’ it says, ‘and become clean’ (Isaiah 1:16): so a prophetic word commanded us long ago.
Palladius: So in the calf, as in an image and in types, the death of Christ, suffered because of us and on our behalf, is sketched in outline.
Cyril: You understand very well. And besides this, I think you would also be struck with wonder if you looked at another point.
Palladius: Which one?

Cyril: If the leader sins, it says, together with those under him, or if the multitude under his hand sins by itself, the victim shall be a calf. But if the leader is caught in faults of his own, let him bring, it says, a he-goat from the goats. And if it is one of the people, the victim shall no longer be male but female. If you like, I will also read the laws on these cases, for it says this: ‘If the ruler sins, and unintentionally does, against any of the commandments of the Lord his God, one thing that ought not to be done, and transgresses, and the sin that he committed in it becomes known to him, he shall bring as his gift a he-goat from the goats, a male without blemish, for the sin. He shall lay his hand on the head of the he-goat, and they shall slaughter it in the place where they slaughter the whole burnt offerings before the Lord; it is a sin offering. And the priest shall put some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger on the horns of the altar of whole burnt offerings, and he shall pour out all its blood at the base of the altar of whole burnt offerings. And he shall offer up all its fat on the altar, like the fat of a peace offering; and the priest shall make atonement for him concerning his sin, and it shall be forgiven him’ (Leviticus 4:22–26). And besides these: ‘If one soul of the people of the land sins unintentionally, by doing, against any of the commandments of the Lord, one thing that ought not to be done, and transgresses, and the sin that he committed in it becomes known to him, he shall bring a she-goat from the goats, a female without blemish; he shall bring it for his sin’ (Leviticus 4:27–28). And after setting out how the sacrifice is to be made, he says: ‘If he brings a sheep as his gift for sin, he shall bring a female without blemish’ (Leviticus 4:32). Do you see, Palladius, the depth of the mystery, sketched for the people of old as in a mirror and in shadows? For the bringing of victims matches, as it were, the size of the transgressions. A calf was offered for ruler and people alike, perhaps because the two had been sick with one common sin; but one kid for one, that is, for one soul. For Christ offered himself for all together, as is pictured in the calf, a weighty and great victim: ‘For where sin abounded,’ it says, ‘grace abounded all the more’ (Romans 5:20). And like a kid and a sheep…
translator_notes: Section opens with -τευμα, the end of πολίτευμα rendered at the close of section 9, so the English begins with the next sentence after an ellipsis. Section ends on the split word προβά|του (‘And like a kid and a sheep…’); the governing phrase δίκην and the rest of the sentence (‘for each one individually…’) fall in section 11. ‘The ash with water’ alludes to the red-heifer rite: Numbers 19:17 LXX has σποδιά with water poured on it (cf. 19:9); Hebrews 9:13 (ash of a heifer sanctifying the defiled) is a possible further echo, not cited. λυτήριον is rendered ‘ransom from sin’ (means of release). The participle ἁγιάζων is masculine, so its subject is the Savior, not the passion; English ‘he sanctifies’. 1 Peter 3:21 (οὐ σαρκὸς ἀπόθεσις ῥύπου) matches exactly. Isaiah 1:16 LXX λούσασθε, καθαροὶ γένεσθε. ἄνωθεν is taken as ‘long ago’ (from of old); ‘from above’ is possible. Palladius’ σκιαγραφεῖται is rendered ‘sketched in outline’. Cyril’s summary distinguishes χίμαρος (he-goat, for the ruler, Leviticus 4:23), χίμαιρα (she-goat, for one of the people, 4:28), and later ἔριφος (kid); the English keeps ‘he-goat’, ‘she-goat’ and ‘kid’ apart. In Leviticus 4:22 LXX ἀκουσίως stands after ἣ οὐ ποιηθήσεται; the English places ‘unintentionally’ with the verb. ἁμαρτίας ἐστί (4:24) is rendered ‘it is a sin offering’. Leviticus 4:29–31 (the manner of the she-goat sacrifice) is summarized by Cyril, not quoted, so no citation. ‘As in a mirror and in shadows’ may echo 1 Corinthians 13:12 and Hebrews 10:1 but is left uncited as doubtful. Romans 5:20 has οὗ where Cyril reads ὅπου; same sense. The dual participle ἠρρωστηκότοιν refers to ruler and people as two parties. ἅμα μὲν ὑπὲρ πάντων rendered ‘for all together’ (not ‘at once’, which could read as ‘immediately’); it pairs with ‘for each one individually’ in section 11.

title: The goat, the sheep, and offerings matched to rank
english: Cyril: …for each one individually, because, I mean, he was made like those under sin and was counted among the lawless, according to the Scriptures (Isaiah 53:12). The kid is a type of the lawless man, since it is fruitless and dry. So Christ sets the saints at his right hand as sheep, and the workers of lawlessness at his left as kids (Matthew 25:33). One may therefore see his glory and surpassing greatness as in the calf; but his being made like us, and his being counted even among the lawless, you will understand through the goat. He was also slain as a sheep, because of his inborn gentleness and the surpassing meekness of the sacrifice. ‘For he was led like a sheep,’ it says, ‘and like a lamb silent before its shearer, so he does not open his mouth’ (Isaiah 53:7). But if the one guilty of the offenses happened to be a ruler, the goat was male (Leviticus 4:22–23); if, however, it was one of the people, a single person, the victim was female, whether it happened to be a sheep or from the goats (Leviticus 4:27–32). Even in the difference between the victims the law points to the wisdom of our Savior’s plan of salvation. For the male always in some way leads and holds first honor, while the female follows and stands second. So the cleansing through Christ is in proportion to each one’s faults, both in those who preside and lead and in those under their authority, each individual subject. For when ruler and people fall into sin they would not be liable to equal charges; the rulers, surely, to greater ones. That is why they are scoured clean by a richer grace.
Palladius: I understand what you mean; for the male is better than the other.

Cyril: And you could see in Christ the difference, as it were, in glory. For he is ruler and, as all confess, the guide of the whole universe, as God and Lord. Yet because of his humanity he also became as it were second in rank, and he was placed under the law (Galatians 4:4), as one who leads the way.
Palladius: The sense is convincing.

Cyril: The law adds other kinds of defilement as well, and once more it has foretold the purification for each, as fulfilled in Christ. It says this: ‘If anyone sins, and hears the voice of adjuration, and he is a witness, having either seen or known, if he does not report it, he shall bear the sin. Whoever touches any unclean thing, whether a carcass, or an unclean thing killed by wild beasts, or the carcasses of unclean abominations, or the carcasses of unclean cattle, or touches human uncleanness, any uncleanness of a person that defiles the one who touches it, and it escaped his notice, but afterwards he knows it and is guilty; or the lawless person who declares with his lips that he will do evil or do good, in anything whatever that a man may declare with an oath, and it is hidden from his eyes, and he comes to know it and sins in any one of these: he shall confess the sin he has committed in this matter, and he shall bring to the Lord for the wrong he has done, for the sin… (Leviticus 5:1–6)
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: §10 ends 'Ἐρίφου δὲ καὶ προβά-' and §11 begins '-του δίκην'. The joined sentence reads: 'And like a kid and a sheep, for each one individually…'. The μέν clause in §10 (Christ offered himself for all, as in the calf) is answered by this δέ clause. 'Counted among the lawless, according to the Scriptures' = Isaiah 53:12 (also quoted in Mark 15:28 and Luke 22:37). 'Made like those under sin' and 'made like us' echo Hebrews 2:17 (ὁμοιωθῆναι) and Romans 8:3, but the wording is Cyril's own; left uncited. Isaiah 53:7 is quoted as printed, without 'to the slaughter' (ἐπὶ σφαγήν), which is in the LXX; possibly abridged by Cyril or the print. The male and female rules summarize Leviticus 4:22–23 (ruler, male goat), 4:27–28 (one of the people, female goat) and 4:32 (female lamb). ὡς ὑφηγούμενος at the end of Cyril's turn is unclear: ὑφηγέομαι normally means 'guide, lead the way'; Cyril may mean that Christ, placed under the law, shows the way for those under it, or he may be playing on ἡγούμενος ('ruler') to suggest a leader who stands in a lower rank. Rendered 'as one who leads the way'. The PDF of PG 68 (col. 968) has the same reading, so there is no variant to choose. Galatians 4:4 cited for 'placed under the law' (γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον). The quotation of Leviticus 5:1–6 follows the LXX closely and runs on into §12; ψυχή rendered 'anyone/whoever/person' in the quotation. οἰκονομία rendered 'plan of salvation'.

title: Confession, the death of Christ, and the poor man’s doves
english: Cyril: …he committed, a female from the flock, a ewe lamb or a she-goat from the goats, for sin; and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he committed, and the sin shall be forgiven him’ (Leviticus 5:6). Observe, then, that the law sets in one equal and identical class of offense the man who hears the voice of adjuration and makes nothing at all of the matter, the man liable for other defilements, and, besides these, the man condemned for perjury. For contempt toward God is truly a monstrous defilement, and it rises to the very extreme of evil; and this offense is near and akin to the uncleannesses of the flesh. Or must we not count accursed perjury and contempt for adjuration as equal?
Palladius: Certainly; for in both cases the charges are always, in a way, evenly matched.

Cyril: Then for these also release will follow through confession and through the slaying of a ewe lamb, that is, a sheep. For, it says, ‘Be the first to tell your lawless deeds, that you may be justified’ (Isaiah 43:26). And the divine David also cries out: ‘I said, I will confess my lawlessness against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the ungodliness of my heart’ (Psalm 32:5). Yet confession alone is not enough to wash us completely clean. It is the death of Christ that sets us entirely free, for he suffered for us and put himself under the sins of us all, as in every kind of domestic animal: I mean in the calf, and in the sheep and the goat. And the law, as if to leave those in defilements and uncleannesses no excuse for neglecting sacrifice, urges anyone who has no calf or sheep to give honor with what is at hand and within his means, saying: ‘If his hand is not strong enough to provide a sheep, he shall bring to the Lord for the sin he committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and one for a whole burnt offering. And he shall bring them to the priest, and the priest shall offer the one for sin first; and the priest shall pinch off its head from the neck, and shall not divide it. And he shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the wall of the altar, and the rest of the blood he shall drain out at the base of the altar; for it is a sin offering. And the second he shall make a whole burnt offering, as is fitting; and the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he committed, and it shall be forgiven him’ (Leviticus 5:7–10). We should compare our Lord Jesus Christ, and very fittingly, to the turtledove and the dove, because the one has the sweetest voice and is the most vocal of birds, and the other comes nearest to the height of meekness. Both were in Christ. For he, the turtledove from above and from heaven, charmed the whole world with the preaching of the Gospel, sending forth, as it were, a clear and sweet song, and making plain the will of God the Father. For as the inspired John says: ‘He whom God has sent speaks the words of God’ (John 3:34). And he also called us to imitate the meekness and gentleness that were in him, saying: ‘Take my yoke… (Matthew 11:29)
translator_notes: Opens inside the quotation of Leviticus 5:1–6 begun in §11 (break at ἁμαρ-|τίας); the English begins at 'that he sinned' and closes the quotation with its citation. Psalm 31:5 in the LXX = Psalm 32:5 in English Bibles. 'Tell your lawless deeds first, that you may be justified' is Isaiah 43:26 LXX (the Hebrew differs). Cyril reads Leviticus 5:4 ('declares with his lips… with an oath') as perjury (ψευδορκία) and puts it on a level with the other cases; that is his reading, kept as he gives it. 'He suffered for us and submitted himself to the sins of us all' may echo Isaiah 53:6 LXX (παρέδωκεν αὐτὸν ταῖς ἁμαρτίαις ἡμῶν) and 1 Peter 2:21; the wording is not close enough to cite. τιμᾶν has no stated object ('to pay his honor'); God is implied but not added. περιστερά rendered 'dove' in Cyril's comparison, 'young pigeons' in the law (νοσσοὶ περιστερῶν). 'The turtledove from above and from heaven' may echo Song of Songs 2:12 LXX ('the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land'); left uncited. The quotation of Matthew 11:29 breaks after 'Take my yoke' (§12) and continues 'upon you' in §13; the citation is placed beside the introductory 'saying' so that it stands with the clause in this section too.

title: The bird not divided, and the flour offering without oil
english: Cyril: …upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart’ (Matthew 11:29). The priest, then, it says, will take the turtledove and nip it with his fingernail (Leviticus 5:8), for that is how light birds are killed. Yet he will not cut it off completely; he clearly means the head. For so the death of Christ was accomplished, not for division but for union. That is why at the beginning, too, when he laid down the law for the Passover, he commanded that the lamb be sacrificed, and yet, he says, ‘It shall be eaten in one house, and you shall not carry any of its flesh outside’ (Exodus 12:46). For Christ is in no way divided (1 Corinthians 1:13); he is one, whole in each and in all. And he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), gathering us into union, both with one another in oneness of soul and, through himself, with God in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). That the death of Christ has brought us not division but union, the bird showed indirectly by being sacrificed without its head being cut clean off the neck. And that he sanctifies the Church with his own blood (Hebrews 13:12) would be signified by the sprinkling of the tent and the things in it with the bird’s blood. One turtledove is for sin, and one, again, for a whole burnt offering; and through both Christ is understood, both dying for us and being offered to the Father as a whole burnt offering for a fragrant aroma (Ephesians 5:2), and offering himself up as the exchange for the life of all.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: The law, moreover, brings the form of the sacrifice down to something very easy to obtain, and commands that it be made in proportion to each person’s means. In this way it cuts away at every point any hesitation over the best offerings, and leaves those who choose slackness without excuse. Again it writes as follows: ‘If his hand cannot find a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, then he shall bring as his gift for the sin he committed a tenth of an ephah of fine flour, for sin. He shall not pour oil on it, nor put frankincense on it, because it is for sin. And he shall bring it to the priest, and the priest, taking from it a full handful, shall lay its memorial portion on the altar of the whole burnt offerings of the Lord; it is a sin offering. And the priest shall make atonement for him for the sin he committed in any one of these, and it shall be forgiven him. And what is left shall belong to the priest, like the offering of fine flour’ (Leviticus 5:11–13). But in these provisions the manner of the sacrifice no longer points to Christ; it hints to us at the life of the one who offers, his approach in Christ, and his consecration to God. For fine flour is offered, the substance from which bread is made, and bread is a type of life. But the law says that it must not be sprinkled with frankincense, nor moistened with oil (Leviticus 5:11), and quite rightly it states beforehand the wise and necessary reason for this: that it is for sin. From sin, gladness, which is understood in the oil, would be utterly and in every way far removed, and so would fragrance, which is perhaps understood in the frankincense. It could not be disputed that the sin in us is truly a gloomy and scentless thing. But there will richly abound…
translator_notes: Opens inside Matthew 11:29, begun at the end of §12. The edition prints the quotation mark after φησίν ('«ὁ ἱερεὺς, καὶ ἀποκνίσει τῷ ὄνυχι…') and never closes it; the words are not a verbatim quotation of Leviticus 5:8 LXX (which has ἀποκνίσει τὴν κεφαλὴν ἀπὸ τοῦ σφονδύλου καὶ οὐ διελεῖ). The fingernail detail and the explanatory clauses ('for that is how light birds are killed', 'that is, the head') read as Cyril's own paraphrase and comment, so they are given without quotation marks; Leviticus 5:8 is cited beside the paraphrase. Exodus 12:46 LXX ('eaten in one house… not carry any of its flesh outside') quoted with small word-order differences. 'Christ is in no way divided' echoes 1 Corinthians 1:13 (μεμέρισται ὁ Χριστός;); 'one, whole in each and in all' may echo Colossians 3:11 but is left uncited. 'Through himself, with God in the Spirit' alludes to Ephesians 2:18. 'Sanctifies… with his own blood' matches Hebrews 13:12 (ἁγιάσῃ διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος τὸν λαόν); Acts 20:28 (the Church bought with his own blood) is a possible second echo. Cyril says the bird's blood is sprinkled on 'the tent and the things in it', though Leviticus 5:9 names the wall of the altar; kept as Cyril has it. 'As a fragrant aroma' (εἰς ὀσμὴν εὐωδίας) = Ephesians 5:2, also the stock LXX sacrificial phrase (e.g. Leviticus 1:9). ἀντάλλαγμα ('exchange') recalls Mark 10:45/Matthew 20:28 in sense but not in wording; left uncited. τοῖς ἑλοῦσι τὸ ῥᾴθυμον read as 'those who choose slackness'. οἶφι = ephah. The last sentence breaks mid-clause: 'Καταπλουτήσει δὲ ἐφ' | ἑαυτῇ, τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀεί πως τὸ ἱλαρόν' (§14), i.e. 'But the gladness of virtue will always richly abound in itself…'; the §13 English ends 'But there will richly abound…' so the §14 translator can complete it.

title: Gladness and fragrance in Christ; restoring stolen holy things
english: Cyril: …in that life, always in some way, the gladness of virtue, as in a spiritual richness; and virtue has much fragrance through hope in God. So the fine flour without frankincense and oil is a type of a life that has no gladness and is bare of fragrance; but in Christ even this life will be changed to gladness. It also receives fragrance in faith and is offered to God through him who scours clean the defiled and spiritually washes those caught in uncleanness. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall take a handful of the fine flour and carry it up to the altar of whole burnt offerings to the Lord’ (Leviticus 5:12). For our approach is in Christ, and through him we who are defiled draw near (Ephesians 2:18). We are justified through faith, and as a pleasing fragrance we offer up to the Father no longer ourselves, but Christ who is in us (Galatians 2:20), since we have the spiritual fragrance (2 Corinthians 2:15).
Palladius: What you say is true.

Cyril: Besides this, if it should happen that some offend God and steal something of what has been consecrated, or go back on what they promised and do not offer it at once, and so through carelessness in these matters incur the charge of forgetfulness, the law cleanses this too. For it is written thus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: If forgetfulness overtakes a soul, and it sins unintentionally in any of the holy things of the Lord, he shall bring for his trespass to the Lord a ram without blemish from the flock, valued in silver shekels by the shekel of the sanctuary, for that in which he trespassed. And what he sinned in the holy things he shall repay, and he shall add a fifth to it and give it to the priest; and the priest shall make atonement for him with the ram of the trespass offering, and he shall be forgiven’ (Leviticus 5:14–16). For it is truly a dreadful thing to steal anything of what has been consecrated and dedicated to the glory of God. In the same way, and on no small charges, failure to pay what was promised will be denounced. For ‘My son,’ it says, ‘if you make a vow to the Lord, do not delay to pay it; it is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay’ (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). And the divinely inspired David sings somewhere: ‘Make vows, and pay them to the Lord your God’ (Psalm 76:11). The sons of Eli too were punished for pilfering some of the holy things and taking for themselves what belonged to God (1 Samuel 2:12–17). What, then, might be the forgiveness for this as well? Or how might one free his foot from the charge and be set free? First, if he makes the repayment richer than what was stolen (‘For he shall add the fifth,’ it says); then, if he brings a purchased ram for sacrifice. This would be a type of Christ, whom the leaders of the Jews in a sense bought for thirty denarii, which they paid to the disciple who betrayed him (Matthew 26:15). So in Christ there is forgiveness for offenses against God as well. And that he would also free us from wrongs done against other people is easy to see for those who have read the law that comes right after this one (Leviticus 6:1–7). It runs thus: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: The soul that sins, and utterly disregards the commandments of the Lord, and lies to his neighbor about a deposit, or about a partnership, or about something seized, or…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §13 ends 'Καταπλουτήσει δὲ ἐφ'' and §14 resumes 'ἑαυτῇ'; the feminine subject is most likely the offerer's life (ζωή, named just before in §13), so the fragment, which completes §13's 'But there will richly abound…', is rendered '…in that life… the gladness of virtue'; 'that life' makes the feminine reflexive's referent explicit. The genitive participle ἐχούσης belongs to ἀρετή, so the fragrance is given to virtue, and ἀεί πως goes with the abounding. 'Πιότης νοητή' (spiritual fatness/richness) answers to the oil, and fragrance to the frankincense. 'Διακαθαίρει πάλιν' has no expressed subject; rendered 'the law cleanses this too', since the next sentence cites the law (could also be Christ). Ephesians 2:18 cited for προσαγωγή + δι' αὐτοῦ; Galatians 2:20 for 'no longer ourselves, but Christ in us'; 2 Corinthians 2:15 for the fragrance of Christ. 'Justified through faith' echoes Romans 5:1 / Galatians 2:16 generally; left uncited. The vow quotation opens with 'Τέκνον' (My son), which is not in LXX Ecclesiastes 5:3-4 (= English 5:4-5); it may blend Ecclesiastes with Deuteronomy 23:21 or sapiential address; cited to Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 (English numbering). 'Vow and pay' is LXX Psalm 75:12 = English Psalm 76:11. Eli's sons: 1 Samuel 2:12-17 (their punishment follows in 2:34 and 4:11). Cyril writes 'thirty denarii' (δηναρίων), not the 'pieces of silver' of Matthew 26:15; kept as he wrote it. 'Ἐκλύσοιεν αἰτίας τὸν πόδα' kept as Cyril's image ('free his foot from the charge'). The Leviticus 6 quotation (LXX 5:20-26 = English 6:1-7) runs on into §15; 'ἁρπαγή' rendered 'something seized' to match 'the plunder he seized' in §15.

title: Restitution to the neighbor; full justification in Christ
english: Cyril: …or has wronged his neighbor in anything, or has found something lost and lies about it, and swears falsely about any one of all the things a man may do so as to sin in them, then it shall be, when he has sinned and trespassed, that he shall give back the plunder he seized, or the wrong he did, or the deposit entrusted to him, or the lost thing he found, in any matter about which he swore falsely; and he shall repay the principal itself and add a fifth to it; to whomever it belongs he shall give it, on the day he is convicted. And for his trespass he shall bring to the Lord a ram without blemish from the flock, at the value of that in which he trespassed. And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord, and he shall be forgiven for any one of all the things he did and in which he trespassed’ (Leviticus 6:2–7). Do you see how the way of cleansing runs alike in both cases and is completed by both means? For he repays with increase, and he brings a ram. The law very rightly commanded that offenses against God and offenses against brothers and kinsmen alike must be put away. But justification in Christ is by no means partial; it is rather a complete washing away of whatever tends to stain us. Therefore he also said: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, he who believes in me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life’ (John 5:24). If, then, the one who through Christ has justification by faith conferred on him has escaped being judged, we are bound to say that he has escaped the charges; and no kind of accusation, I say, could prevail against such a person. For ‘it is God who justifies; who is he that condemns?’ (Romans 8:33–34). So when we answer with deeds to those brothers who have been grieved, we shall find justification in Christ close at hand. So also Zacchaeus the tax collector, when called to apostleship, promised not only that he would follow the one who had called him, but also that he would give back fourfold whatever he had taken by wrong (Luke 19:8). For I think that those who are to make Christ dwell within themselves through the Spirit (Ephesians 3:16–17) must first wash off their filth and first scour away their offenses, and so show him their own soul bright and spotless, just as the divinely inspired Psalmist, having reached this fine state of virtue, cried aloud: ‘My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I will sing and make melody’ (Psalm 57:7). For just as dyes settle into wool when it is clean, but if any trace of dirt remains, what was taken in is at once easily shed and finds no firm hold in it, so too participation in Christ sinks into holy and pure souls, but would not settle at all in those that are not so. ‘For the Holy Spirit of wisdom will flee from deceit,’ as it is written, ‘and will not dwell in a body in debt to sins’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:4–5). So by making amends to those who have been wronged, and by good deeds that lead to friendship and shear away our brothers’ grief, we shall free ourselves from every charge and gain the forgiveness that is in Christ.
Palladius: You have spoken most rightly.
translator_notes: Opens mid-quotation of Leviticus 6 (LXX 5:21-26 = English 6:2-7), continued from §14. 'Δι' ἀμφοῖν' taken as the two means (restitution with a fifth, and the ram). The John quotation reads 'ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμέ', which matches John 6:47 rather than John 5:24 ('he who hears my word and believes him who sent me'); the rest of the verse is John 5:24, so cited there. 'Εἰσποιητήν' (adoptive, brought in from outside) rendered 'conferred on him': justification as given, not one's own. Romans 8:33-34 is given in Cyril's short form. Zacchaeus 'κεκλημένος εἰς ἀποστολήν' is rendered 'called to apostleship' as written; Luke does not say he followed or became an apostle. 'Christ dwelling within through the Spirit' cited to Ephesians 3:16-17 as a clear allusion. 'Μελῳδός' (the Melodist) rendered 'the Psalmist'. 'My heart is ready' is LXX Psalm 56:8 = English Psalm 57:7 (the same words recur at LXX 107:2 = English 108:1). The Wisdom quotation blends Wisdom of Solomon 1:5 ('a holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit') and 1:4 ('will not dwell in a body enslaved to sin'), with 'σοφίας' for 'παιδείας'; rendered 'the Holy Spirit of wisdom' because Cyril applies it to the indwelling Spirit through whom Christ dwells in us (a reader may prefer lower case for the Wisdom text itself). 'Ἀποκείροντες' (shearing away) keeps Cyril's wool image from the dye simile. 'Λύπας' rendered 'grief' (not 'grievances'), matching 'τοῖς λελυπημένοις' (those who have been grieved); the Greek names no agent for the grieving or the wronging, so none is added.

title: Bodily uncleanness as a type of the soul; testing for leprosy
english: Cyril: Shall we, then, add still other lines of thought to these, and explain both the charges that arise from defilements and what has been decreed for the cleansing of each?
Palladius: By all means; for in this way our discussion of it would bring us a more abundant benefit.

Cyril: It is written, then, in Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out of the camp every leper, and everyone who has a discharge, and everyone unclean through contact with the dead; male and female alike, send them out of the camp, and they shall not defile their camps, in which I dwell among them’ (Numbers 5:1–3). Now it is clear to anyone, I think, that the law could not reasonably be thought to rebuke us in these matters for what happens by necessity and against our will. For why should a bodily affliction be punished, and how could the one who has fallen into fleshly infirmities justly incur the law’s condemnation? It is wise, then, and necessary to take these bodily conditions as an image and type of the diseases in souls. For in this way the law would be spiritual (Romans 7:14), and what God has declared on each matter at various times would be a holy verdict, not subjecting to penalties those caught by diseases they did not choose, but those in whose case the fact of wrongdoing would make the rebuke holy.
Palladius: How well you put it.

Cyril: He commanded, then, that the leper be sent away from the camp, yet in his case he makes the examination very exact, and orders that the disease be tested, saying: ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: If a man has on the skin of his body a scar with a bright mark, and an infection of leprosy appears in the skin of his body, he shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons the priests. And the priest shall look at the infection in the skin of his body; and if the hair in the infection has turned white, and the infection appears deeper than the skin of the body, it is an infection of leprosy; and the priest shall look and pronounce him unclean (Leviticus 13:1–3). But if it is bright white in the skin of his body, and it does not appear deeper than the skin, and its hair has not turned white, but it is faint, then the priest shall isolate the infection for seven days. And the priest shall look at the infection on the seventh day; and if in his sight the infection remains as it was and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall isolate him for seven days a second time, and the priest shall look at him on the seventh day a second time. And if the infection is faint and has not spread in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him clean, for it is a mark. And when he has washed his clothes he shall be clean (Leviticus 13:4–6). But if the mark changes and spreads in the skin after the priest has seen him in order to pronounce him clean, he shall show himself to the priest a second time; and the priest shall look at him, and if the mark has spread in the skin, the priest shall pronounce him unclean (Leviticus 13:7–8);…
translator_notes: Numbers 5:1-3 LXX 'ἀκάθαρτον ἐπὶ ψυχῇ' is the standard idiom for corpse defilement; rendered 'unclean through contact with the dead'. 'Πνευματικὸς ὁ νόμος' is a clear allusion to Romans 7:14. 'Μιανεῖ' / 'καθαριεῖ' rendered 'pronounce unclean / clean' (the priest's declaration). 'Ἁφή' rendered 'infection', 'σημασία' 'mark', 'ἀμαυρά' 'faint', 'μεταπίπτω' 'spread' (as in standard English Leviticus). Leviticus 13 numbering is the same in LXX and English. The quotation is cut mid-verse: Leviticus 13:8 ends in §17 with 'λέπρα ἐστίν' (it is leprosy), so the last citation is placed inside the open quotation. 'ταπεινὴ ἀπὸ δέρματος' rendered 'deeper than the skin', since Cyril's §17 explanation turns on depth; 'ἐναντίον αὐτοῦ' rendered 'in his sight'; 'σημασία γάρ ἐστι' kept as 'for it is a mark' without an added 'only'.

title: Leprosy and the white patch: first the plain sense, then the spiritual
english: Cyril: …it is leprosy.’ (Leviticus 13:8) The matter, Palladius, turns on fine distinctions, and the account of these things is not easy to grasp. Yet I think I must gather my mind and say in a few words what the law means to show. But first I will explain how the conditions differ. Leprosy is a most grievous disease of human bodies, hard to escape and devouring, and it comes about by a deadening. The sore is hollowed out at once, as the skin is consumed and keeps sinking deeper, since the corruption always creeps downward. That, I think, is why the hair growing on those places withers and turns white, and like a plant it perishes along with the soil beneath it. Such, then, is leprosy. The white patch, on the other hand, is a bodily ailment that resembles leprosy, except that it does not drive the harm deep or send the feeling of the disease into the parts within. It floats, as it were, on the surface and barely blooms on the body. It does not turn the hair white, nor does it spread beyond control; with very few remedies it is easily reined in, and the flesh where it broke out returns to health. So leprosy is an undoubted deadness, while the white patch raises some suspicion of leprosy but is not in truth the same thing, that is, leprosy and deadness. The law therefore condemns the leper as unclean, since he has already suffered deadness; but it acquits of the charge the one sick with the white patch, since he has come under suspicion of leprosy but is not actually leprous. This is why it says that if there is a scar with a mark, and a leprous sore, and the skin looks hollowed, and the hair also changes to white, dying, it may be, together with the flesh beneath it, then it will certainly be leprosy (Leviticus 13:2–3); for the deadness creeps deep. But if there is a white patch with a mark, without any hollowing of the skin and without the hair changing to white, let it be tested, it says, by the priest, and let the man be set apart a second time (Leviticus 13:4–5). For it is not unlikely that the passing of the days itself, putting the ailment to the test, may sometimes show the exact truth to those who examine it. In one case the hair takes on another color as the skin hollows, and the white patch has turned into leprosy. But if none of these things has happened, ‘let him be released,’ it says, ‘from the charge’ (Leviticus 13:6). For the condition is not leprosy, but something that resembles leprosy and comes very close to it, namely the white patch. The plain sense, then, and the explanation of the matter have been set out well enough. But come, let us speak of the spiritual meaning and lay hold of the ideas that are hidden and grasped by the mind.
Palladius: How fine and helpful that is!

Cyril: We who are being made alive in Christ (and by making alive I mean the spiritual kind) must depart from dead works (Hebrews 9:14) and go as far from them as we can. These, I think, would be the works through which the soul is put to death and the mind grows cold, when it has turned without restraint toward the things of the flesh and of the world. For if it is true that ‘the one who sows to the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh’ (Galatians 6:8), and that those who live according to the flesh…
translator_notes: Opens inside the Leviticus 13:1–8 quotation begun in §16; the closing words ‘it is leprosy’ are the end of Leviticus 13:8 in the LXX. λεύκη is rendered ‘white patch’ throughout (a superficial white skin ailment distinct from λέπρα); ἁφή is rendered ‘sore’ (LXX ‘touch/stroke’, KJV ‘plague’). Cyril’s summaries of the test (Leviticus 13:2–6) are paraphrase, not quotation; ‘let him be released from the charge’ paraphrases the priest’s pronouncing clean in Leviticus 13:6. ‘Dead works’ (νεκρῶν ἔργων) is cited to Hebrews 9:14 as a clear verbal echo; Hebrews 6:1 has the same phrase. The section ends mid-sentence: ‘and those who live according to the flesh’ continues in §18 with ‘cannot please God’. ἀποψύχεσθαι νοῦν rendered ‘the mind grows cold’ (LSJ: faint, lose breath; be chilled).

title: Sin carried into deeds is the soul's leprosy; bare desire is the white patch
english: Cyril: …cannot please God (Romans 8:8), how, or on what ground, could anyone still doubt that they will also die (Romans 8:13)? The one, then, who is defiled in soul and mind, and is full of the world’s wickedness, is dead, held fast in the works of deadness. And if anyone chose to call such a state a leprosy of the mind in the true sense, he would not miss the right word. Such a person, then, is unclean in the eyes of Christ. ‘For the priest,’ it says, ‘shall pronounce him unclean’ (Leviticus 13:3). For at the divine judgment seat, counted among those who dearly love sin, he will hear: ‘Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you’ (Matthew 7:23; Luke 13:27; Matthew 25:41). But to the white patch and the scar with a mark we should liken those who are still at the stage of mere desire and have not yet carried their thought into action. Or do you not agree that it is true that pleasures and thoughts spring up in us ahead of the deeds, and dawn, as it were, before them, calling us toward something the law condemns?
Palladius: I agree, for I recall the blessed David saying: ‘Before I was brought low, I did wrong’ (Psalm 119:67).

Cyril: You have spoken most rightly. Before the deeds are done, the mind has certainly already fallen into wrongdoing, having first been in labor with the pleasure. Yet while the sin still lies only in desires, the mind stands between the two and looks toward both. It is free to lean toward whichever it may choose; it has not yet suffered deadness, though it has come very near to the evil and is in labor with the passion. The Savior’s disciple has clearly told us something of this kind: ‘Let no one,’ he says, ‘when he is tempted, say, “I am tempted by God”; for God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is completed, brings forth death’ (James 1:13–15).
Palladius: True.

Cyril: So being wholly dead, as in leprosy (I mean the leprosy of the mind) and as in the condition of deadness that comes from sin, would perhaps come about not in desires alone but when they issue in deeds. As long as the evil is still in the mind’s birth pangs, there is not yet deadness and not yet death, for ‘not every sin leads to death,’ as the Savior’s disciple has said (1 John 5:16–17). There is still only a suspicion that it may suffer the things that can bring death. And we said that the white patch looks like leprosy, or comes near to it. ‘The priest shall look,’ it says, at the one held by the condition (I mean the white patch); and if it is seen not to be changing into leprosy, he shall not pronounce him unclean, but rather shall set him apart (Leviticus 13:4–5). For before God it is not beyond rebuke even to dwell in desires and come near to evil. But if the condition, it says, resists the change and has not turned toward the worse, ‘let him be clean’ (Leviticus 13:6). Best, then, and truly saving, is to refuse deadness, I mean the deadness that lies in deeds…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence from §17. ‘Those who live according to the flesh cannot please God’ blends Romans 8:8 (οἱ ἐν σαρκὶ ὄντες) with Romans 8:13 (εἰ κατὰ σάρκα ζῆτε, μέλλετε ἀποθνῄσκειν); both cited. ‘Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness; I do not know you’ is a conflation: πορεύεσθε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ (Matthew 25:41), ἐργάται ἀνομίας/ἀδικίας with οὐκ οἶδα ὑμᾶς (Luke 13:27), οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν (Matthew 7:23); all three cited. Psalm 118:67 LXX = Psalm 119:67 English; LXX ἐπλημμέλησα rendered ‘I did wrong’ so that Cyril’s next word, πλημμελείαις (‘wrongdoing’), keeps the link. ‘Not every sin leads to death’ is a paraphrase of 1 John 5:16–17, which Cyril assigns to ‘the Savior’s disciple’. The birth-pang language (προωδινήσας, ὠδῖσιν) may echo Psalm 7:14 LXX, but is left uncited as doubtful. The rules about the white patch are paraphrases of Leviticus 13:4–6. The section ends mid-sentence and continues in §19.
