title: Washing as a type of baptism; the law reverses itself on total leprosy
english: Cyril: …and that already, in some way, chills the mind in the very deeds themselves. Besides this, it is wise to try hard to turn away from the passions even when they are still seen only as desires; for this, I think, is to depart from both leprosy itself and the white patch. For you have learned that Emmanuel, who is God by nature, our great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), counts our affairs worthy of the closest oversight. He welcomes those who have washed away what is evil, but sends out of the camp of the saints those he sees to be defiled (Numbers 5:2–3).
Palladius: What you say is true.

Cyril: ‘For you shall be holy,’ it says, ‘because I am holy’ (Leviticus 11:44; 1 Peter 1:16). And notice that the law says that the one freed from the charge will be clean once he has washed his clothes (Leviticus 13:6). In this the law foretells the cleansing through water, and, as in types that the bodily senses can perceive, it sketches for us the mystery of holy baptism.
Palladius: I understand.
Cyril: See, then, Palladius, how very searching the law is. It shifts our thoughts, as it were, to the opposite case, and in every way it hints at what leads to our benefit.
Palladius: What do you mean?

Cyril: For it said again: ‘If a leprous sore appears in a person, he shall come to the priest. The priest shall look, and behold, there is a white scar in the skin, and it has turned the hair white, and there is some healthy, living flesh in the scar. It is a chronic leprosy in the skin of his body; the priest shall pronounce him unclean and shall set him apart, because he is unclean. But if the leprosy breaks out widely in the skin of his body, and the leprosy covers all the skin of the sore from his head to his feet, as far as the priest can see, then the priest shall look, and behold, the leprosy has covered all the skin of his body; and the priest shall pronounce him clean of the sore, because it has all turned white, and he is clean. But on whatever day living flesh appears in him, he shall be unclean. The priest shall look at the healthy flesh and pronounce him unclean. The healthy flesh is unclean; it is leprosy. But if the healthy flesh is restored and turns white, he shall come to the priest; the priest shall look, and behold, the sore has turned white; and the priest shall pronounce the sore clean, and he is clean’ (Leviticus 13:9–17).
Palladius: And how are we to understand the reversal here?
Cyril: Do you not understand that we affirmed leprosy to be a partial deadness in living flesh, and that the one held by the disease was cast out as defiled?
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: Look, then: the matter is somehow turned round for us again to its opposite. For if, it says, a man becomes wholly leprous, held fast by deadness, with nothing healthy in him, then let him be released from the charges of…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence from §18. ‘Great High Priest’ cited to Hebrews 4:14 (ἀρχιερέα μέγαν). Emmanuel is used as a title of Christ (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23) and is left uncited as a name, not a quotation. ‘Sends out of the camp’ points back to Numbers 5:2–3, quoted in §16. ‘You shall be holy, because I am holy’: the word order ὅτι ἐγὼ ἅγιός εἰμι matches 1 Peter 1:16; the source is Leviticus 11:44 (also 11:45; 19:2; 20:7). The washing of clothes is Leviticus 13:6. The long quotation is Leviticus 13:9–17 LXX. In 13:11 the LXX text Cyril quotes says the priest ‘shall set him apart’ (ἀφοριεῖ), whereas the Hebrew and most English Bibles say he ‘shall not shut him up’; the translation follows Cyril’s Greek. ἀπὸ τοῦ ὑγιοῦς τῆς σαρκὸς τῆς ζώσης (13:10) rendered ‘some healthy, living flesh’ (Hebrew: raw flesh); χρώς rendered ‘flesh’ to keep Cyril’s living/dead contrast. ἐντενές rendered ‘searching’ (intent, exacting). The section ends mid-sentence; ‘defilement: he is clean’ opens §20.

title: Why total leprosy is clean: dead to sin and alive to God
english: Cyril: …defilement: he is clean (Leviticus 13:13). But if any trace of living flesh remains in him, ‘let the priest,’ it says, ‘record his uncleanness’; for the living flesh will make him unclean, and he is a leper (Leviticus 13:14–15). This case too will count the same as the charges of leprosy.
Palladius: I cannot understand what you mean. If partial leprosy makes people unclean, how could complete and total leprosy declare them clean?

Cyril: The matter, Palladius, turns on fine distinctions. But we shall by no means suppose that the precision of the law brings in an interpretation that fights against itself and, as it were, marches against us. To each case a reason has been fitted that is wise and necessary and beyond reproach. Come, let us state it, if you agree.
Palladius: By all means; you will be speaking most welcome words to one who thirsts for them.

Cyril: In two ways, I think, we shall achieve the life that is most lawful in the sight of God, who loves virtue. Either, living for him, we refuse the deadness that comes from passions and sin, and this is not to suffer leprosy; for a partial deadness befalling a living body is what makes leprosy. Or, in the other way, through a good deadness, and by no longer consenting to live in a worldly way, we shall bind on, like a crown, the vote of approval awarded to all that is best. For the inspired Paul writes thus to some: ‘So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus’ (Romans 6:11). Living in Christ, then, by striving to accomplish what pleases him, we shall hate being put to death, plainly, by passions and sins; and having died to sin, as it is written (Romans 6:2), we shall thrust away living in it, because we think rightly.
Palladius: Explain this to me still more clearly, for I do not understand it very well.

Cyril: Do we not say, Palladius, that Christ endured death for us for this reason: so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and was raised for them, that is, for Christ (2 Corinthians 5:15)?
Palladius: We do; it is agreed.

Cyril: So we live for Christ when we order our lives by the Gospel and loathe the deadness that comes from sin, that is, the death that comes from the passions. Indeed the inspired Peter writes of Christ: ‘He bore our sins in his body on the tree, so that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness’ (1 Peter 2:24). For I think that those who care to live a shining life must go far from everything that can bring death, and must succeed in ridding themselves of defilements.
Palladius: You speak well.
Cyril: So he would least of all suffer, as in leprosy, the…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence from §19 (‘let him be released from the charges that bring defilement: he is clean’), a paraphrase of Leviticus 13:12–13; the citation sits on ‘he is clean’ (13:13). ‘Let the priest record his uncleanness’ (καταγραφέτω) is Cyril’s paraphrase of Leviticus 13:14–15, not LXX wording. ‘As it is written’ after ‘having died to sin’ points to Romans 6:2 (οἵτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ), which Cyril quotes in full in §21. πολιτευόμενοι εὐαγγελικῶς (‘live as citizens of the Gospel’) may echo Philippians 1:27; left uncited as doubtful. The crown image is Cyril’s own and is not cited. θεσπέσιος (of Paul and Peter) rendered ‘inspired’. ψῆφον ‘verdict’ (vote of approval) for ‘all that is best’. ‘A shining life’ renders διαβιῶναι λαμπρῶς (to live brilliantly, splendidly). The section ends mid-sentence: §21 supplies the noun (πάθος, ‘condition’) and the subject (‘the one who has chosen to live for Christ’).

title: Dead to sin, alive to God; leprosy in healed sores and burns
english: Cyril: …condition: the one who has chosen to live for Christ and follows the commands of the Gospel, while thrusting away the deadness that comes from sin.
Palladius: I am convinced.

Cyril: This, then, is one way in which we can please God; and there is another that may in turn be rightly carried out, as follows. For we must put to death our members that are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire and covetousness (Colossians 3:5), and so seem in some way already to have died to sin, and that completely, no longer living in it. The divine Paul will assure us of this when he says: ‘What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? By no means! How shall we who died to sin still live in it?’ (Romans 6:1–2). So then, just as in the case of one who has chosen to live for Christ the law made being partly dead liable to its penalties, so too in the case of one who has died to sin, to live in it would again be a defilement, and one not free of the charge the law brings. For this reason it says that if leprosy should cover the whole body, a kind of deadness spreading over every member, it would signify the one who has died to sin; and there is no longer defilement in the body (Leviticus 13:12–13). For he is clean, it says, who has died to sin wholly and utterly, who has given it no place, and has not, as it were, let it lodge within him. ‘But if,’ it says, ‘living flesh should again be seen in him, the living flesh will defile him’ (Leviticus 13:14–15). For to live for sin at all, even in part, makes the sick man abominable. ‘For a little leaven,’ it says, ‘leavens the whole lump’ (1 Corinthians 5:6; Galatians 5:9), and the saying is true. But if, it says, the living flesh should be restored and change back to leprosy, let the charges be dropped: he is clean (Leviticus 13:16–17). For he has been freed even from still living partly for sin, since his mind has moved over to the deadness that is praised and has made a truly excellent change. So then, to sum up what I have said: if we live for God, let nothing be dead in us; if we have died to sin, let nothing of sin be alive in us. For this is the bright road for us of a way of life fit for saints, one with nothing in it open to reproach.
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: The law marks off such conditions still more finely. ‘And if there should be,’ it says, ‘a suspicion and appearance of leprosy, perhaps in a wound that has scarred over, or in a part of the body that was once burned, let the priest again use the same close scrutiny and examination. And if the white spot that seemed to break out has not changed into leprosy, let him be clean,’ it says; ‘but if there should be a clear change of the white spot into leprosy, he will be unclean and abominable’ (Leviticus 13:18–28). By these things too the law hints to us that if the sicknesses in our souls (and they are countless), once healed by gentle treatment and at times brought, as it were, to scar over, should somehow be raked open by our carelessness, the one who will examine them is…
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: §20 ends 'So he would least of all suffer the [condition] as in leprosy'; the first word here (πάθος) completes that clause, rendered 'condition'. 'καὶ οἱονεί πως ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸ ἐναυλίζεσθαι δούς' has no negation of its own; the sense requires the negation of the preceding 'τόπον οὐδένα' to carry over ('has not let it lodge within him'), otherwise the clause contradicts its context; a dropped μηδέ is possible. Leviticus 13 quotations are Cyril's free paraphrase of the LXX: 13:14-15 LXX has 'χρὼς ζῶν ... μιανθήσεται' and 'ὁ χρὼς ὁ ὑγιής'; 13:16-17 LXX says the healthy flesh 'turns white', where Cyril says 'changes to leprosy' (rendered 'change back to leprosy'). The 'suspicion or appearance' passage is a summary paraphrase of 13:18-23 (healed boil, ἕλκος) and 13:24-28 (burn, κατάκαυμα); cited as a range. 'Little leaven' is word for word in both 1 Corinthians 5:6 and Galatians 5:9; both cited. Final clause breaks off; §22 supplies the subject 'Christ, our great High Priest', so the English ends 'the one who will examine them is…' to keep the active voice across the break.

title: Christ judges a relapse; leprosy of the head and beard
english: Cyril: …Christ, our great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), and he will give a very just verdict. For if the disease has gone no further, it says, than thoughts alone, the one who suffers it is by no means free of rebuke, for he will be set apart (Leviticus 13:21); yet he is not cast out entirely, nor is he wholly dead. But if the passion should shoot through the thoughts and through desire itself, having already undergone in some way a complete change for the worse, it will make the one who has fallen sick again liable to the penalties for defilement (Leviticus 13:22). So we must guard above all against waking passions that have already been lulled to sleep, against reopening the wounds of the mind, and against running back to where we were at the beginning. Otherwise we too shall hear a saint crying aloud: ‘What the true proverb says has happened to them: The dog returns to its own vomit, and the sow, after washing, to wallowing in the mire’ (2 Peter 2:22).
Palladius: You seem to me to speak rightly and very reasonably.

Cyril: This is what the law tells us about leprosy and about leprosy in scars and wounds. But it goes further and says: ‘And if a man or a woman has a mark of leprosy on the head or in the beard, the priest shall look at the head’ (Leviticus 13:29–30). ‘And if there is,’ it says, ‘a hollow in it, where the skin is wasting and sinking in, and also a change of the hair to whiteness, such a person is a leper and will be unclean,’ it says, ‘beyond dispute’ (Leviticus 13:30). ‘But if none of these signs appears, let the one who has the white patch shave his head or his beard,’ it says. ‘And when his hair has been stripped away in this way, let him come to the priest and be examined then. For if the mark, that is, the white spot, has not spread wide but stays, as it were, in its place, or has grown smaller, let him be clean again. For the condition is not leprosy, but rather a suspicion and an appearance of it’ (Leviticus 13:31–37).
Palladius: What, then, would be the meaning of these things too?

Cyril: Defilement in us is twofold, Palladius: of the flesh and of the spirit (2 Corinthians 7:1). The flesh is stained by its own outrageous and unholy passions; the soul and the mind are stained above all by straying from right doctrine to worse things and by the corruption of sound faith, and besides these by tricks and deceits, false oaths, gossip, conceit, quarrels, jealousies (2 Corinthians 12:20), and whatever lies near these and is akin to them and stands equally accused of wickedness. So in these things the law seems perhaps to be calling to mind the passions of the soul, and to wish to point out the sicknesses that usually arise in the mind. For the head is a type of the mind, and the beard a type of wise understanding, since the beard too is a sign of maturity. So the High Priest of all, that is, Christ, watches over our affairs and examines them closely; he will look into the mind itself and test the inward and hidden heart. And if there should be any corruption and alteration, either from right belief to what is not right, or into baseness of character and the malice that is most…
translator_notes: 'ὁ μέγας ἡμῶν ἀρχιερεύς' echoes Hebrews 4:14 (ἀρχιερέα μέγαν); cited. 'φησί' in the thought-versus-desire sentence introduces Cyril's own reading of the law, not a quotation; the citations mark only the clear echoes 'he will be set apart' (LXX Leviticus 13:21 ἀφοριεῖ, also 13:26) and the spreading that makes him unclean (13:22, also 13:27). The head-and-beard passage paraphrases LXX Leviticus 13:29-37 (the θραῦσμα, scall): the LXX speaks of thin yellow hair (θρὶξ ξανθίζουσα) and shaving around the mark, where Cyril has hair turning white and shaving the head or beard; his wording is translated as he gives it. The source's quotation marks are uneven (no close after 'δόκησις'); the paraphrase is closed at 'appearance of it'. The vice list (ψιθυρισμοί, φυσιώσεις, ἔριδες, ζῆλοι) is drawn from 2 Corinthians 12:20; cited as an allusion. 'δοκιμάσει φρένας' may echo Jeremiah 17:10 or Psalm 7:9 (LXX 7:10) but the wording differs; left uncited. Section ends mid-word (κακοβουλίαν τὴν αὐ|τῷ μάλιστα κατεστυγημένην); English breaks at 'most…' and §23 resumes 'hateful to him'.

title: Sickness of the mind; God sees all; small faults forgiven
english: Cyril: …hateful to him, he will drive them off again as defiled and pass the sentence that makes them wholly unclean. This, I say, is what it means to suffer leprosy on the head or on the beard. But if the mind is, as it were, at the beginning of its sickness, yet is not seen to have turned aside entirely into the sickness I spoke of, he is set apart and made subject to measured rebukes, but he will not be wholly unclean, nor estranged from God; when he has washed his garments he will be clean (Leviticus 13:34), that is, he will receive as his help the justification that is in Christ. And the shaving of the hair, which lays the wound bare before the priest, would signify that everything, as it were, is cleared out of the way, and that whatever he may wish to look upon lies bare and unhindered before the eyes of the Godhead. ‘For there is no creature hidden from his sight, but all things are naked and laid open to his eyes,’ as it is written (Hebrews 4:13).
Palladius: That is true. For he said somewhere through the voice of a saint: ‘I am a God who is near, and not a God far off. Shall anything be hidden from me?’ (Jeremiah 23:23–24).

Cyril: Look, Palladius, how much more finely still the law speaks. It passes over nothing needed for knowledge without bringing it under its own rules, and so it benefits those who listen. ‘For no one will understand his faults,’ as it is written (Psalm 19:12), ‘and we all stumble in many ways’ (James 3:2). For our nature suffers from weakness and from slipping easily into wrongdoing; and ‘No one is clean from filth,’ as Holy Scripture says, ‘not even if his life on earth were a single day’ (Job 14:4–5). This is why the divine David sings to us: ‘If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand? For with you is propitiation’ (Psalm 130:3–4). See, then, how the law kindly drops the charge against us for faults like these, and in its gentleness cleanses those who, through human slipping, have fallen into lapses that are bitter and all but involuntary. For it says this: ‘And if a man or a woman has in the skin of his flesh bright spots, shining and whitish, the priest shall look, and there in the skin of his flesh are bright spots, shining and whitish, it is a white rash; it breaks out in the skin of his flesh; he is clean’ (Leviticus 13:38–39). And yet, if one looks into the matter strictly, to have a white rash would be a disease of the flesh and close to leprosy. But it does not suffer deadness, nor is it past all hope. Our faults are something like this: they are admittedly sicknesses, but not to the point of death and the ruin of the soul. The Judge does not examine too strictly, because ‘he knows how we were formed’ (Psalm 103:14), and he was not unaware of the weakness of our nature. So he grants forgiveness out of his innate love for humankind. And this, I think, is what is meant by ‘A white rash is clean’ (Leviticus 13:39). But sometimes small faults befall the mind even of good people: for example, brief fits of irritation, moderate stirrings toward anger, impatience with our brothers, and at times a craving for empty…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word: §22 'κακοβουλίαν τὴν αὐ-' + §23 'τῷ μάλιστα κατεστυγημένην' = 'the malice most hateful to him'. 'Washed his garments, clean' is LXX Leviticus 13:34 (πλυνάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια καθαρὸς ἔσται; also 13:6). 'The justification that is in Christ' is not cited: no single verse is quoted (cf. Romans 3:24, Galatians 2:17). LXX renumbering: Psalm 18:13 LXX = Psalm 19:12 English; Psalm 129:3-4 LXX = Psalm 130:3-4; Psalm 102:14 LXX = Psalm 103:14. Cyril turns the Psalm's question 'who will understand faults?' into a statement ('no one will understand') and joins it to James 3:2 under one 'as it is written'; both cited. Job 14:4-5 follows the LXX, whose wording differs from the Hebrew-based English text of those verses. Jeremiah 23:23-24 LXX numbering equals the English here; Cyril's last clause ('shall anything be hidden from me?') condenses LXX 23:24. ἱλασμός rendered 'propitiation' to keep the doctrinal term. ἀλφός (LXX Leviticus 13:39, a harmless dull-white eruption) rendered 'white rash'. 'Not unto death' (οὐκ εἰς θάνατον) may echo 1 John 5:16-17 or John 11:4; doubtful, uncited. ὀλιγοψυχίαι πρὸς ἀδελφούς rendered 'impatience with our brothers' (Lampe gives both 'faintheartedness' and 'impatience'). Section ends mid-word (δοξα|ρίων); English breaks at 'empty…' and §24 resumes 'little honors'.

title: Baldness is clean: small human faults, and anger to be checked
english: Cyril: …little honors, and passions of that kind; and these are apt at times to befall even those whose life is blameless and who are truly pure. For they are human, and in a way common to all who spend their life in flesh and blood. So the law sketches these too, again in a figure, and says this: ‘If anyone’s head loses its hair, he is bald; he is clean. And if his head loses its hair at the front, he is bald on the forehead; he is clean’ (Leviticus 13:40–41). The involuntary loss of hair would be a condition of the head; and we were saying just now that the head is named as a type of the mind, for the head is the dwelling place of the mind, at least in the opinion of some.
Palladius: I will remember.

Cyril: So the conditions of the bodily head would fittingly show the sicknesses of the mind, small ones again, and of the kind it is right to pardon. Therefore the law releases us from every human passion and from the involuntary defilements that may befall us, since our nature cannot help suffering weakness; and to be wholly freed from passions does not belong to the present time, but would befit the age to come, when sin will be shaken from its foundations and we shall pass over into a life wholly free from harm. ‘But if,’ it says, ‘there should be a scar with a reddish mark on the bald head or on the bald forehead, he is a leper and will be unclean’ (Leviticus 13:42–44). For sometimes even small passions run on until they carry the weight of offenses, and they defile terribly when we do not cut them short and they have gained, as it were, an open passage toward worse things, one wholly unrebuked. I mean something like this: someone is sometimes a little angry, and the passion has taken hold in him, as happens to a human being. Let it be cut short by gentle means, so that the small fault may not grow until, little by little, a charge that leads to death is found against those who suffer it. This is what is meant when leprosy happens to break out on a bald head: the slide from nothing toward worse things, taking place, as it were, in a type. So I say that this was rightly spoken by blessed David: ‘Be angry, and do not sin’ (Psalm 4:4).
Palladius: How profound the argument is!

Cyril: Very much so. For you notice, I think, that I am speaking with great subtlety, and that I cannot either grasp or put into words such insights without sweat. But that those who suffer the unholy sickness of open offenses cannot escape notice, even though the smallest and hidden faults sometimes go unnoticed, you will learn from this as well. Those who have become bald, it says, are clean, as you will remember; the law rightly pardons us our small stumbles, as we were saying just now. But if leprosy should appear on someone’s bald head, that is, when the passion is carried from small things to worse, then, then indeed it says that he becomes conspicuous and disgraceful, with no word to plead for him against the charges…
translator_notes: Opens mid-word: §23 'κενῶν ... δοξα-' + §24 'ρίων ἔφεσις' = 'a craving for empty little honors'. Leviticus 13:40-41 follows the LXX closely. The reddish mark (13:42-44) is paraphrased: LXX 13:42 has 'ἁφὴ λευκὴ ἢ πυρρίζουσα' (a white or reddish mark), Cyril 'οὐλὴ σημασίας πυρρίζουσα'. LXX Psalm 4:5 = Psalm 4:4 English; the same words appear in Ephesians 4:26, but Cyril names David, so only the Psalm is cited. 'γραφὴ πρὸς θάνατον' ('a charge that leads to death') may echo 1 John 5:16; doubtful, uncited. 'ἀναμνήσει' read as second person middle future ('you will remember'), answering Palladius' 'I will remember'; it could also be third person ('it will remind'). 'ἐν ἀνθρώπῳ' read as 'as happens to a human being'. Section ends mid-sentence; §25 opens with 'δυνάμενον' ('able'), which completes 'no word ... able to plead for him'; the English ends 'with no word to plead for him against the charges…'.

title: The leper outside the camp and the cloth given to the fire
english: Cyril: …that could plead its case. That is why it says: ‘And the leper who has the affliction must have his garments unfastened and his head uncovered; he must cover his mouth, and he shall be called unclean. All the days that the affliction is on him he is unclean, and unclean he shall remain; he shall live apart, and his dwelling shall be outside the camp’ (Leviticus 13:45–46). The unfastened garments and the uncovered head would indicate quite clearly that he is disgraced with nothing to hide it. The covering of the mouth means that he has, so to speak, no defense and can say nothing when God charges him with his uncleanness. And the requirement that he leave the camp would again be a type of his no longer living among the choirs of the saints, but, banished as it were from the holy assembly, having no share in any good thing.
Palladius: What a dreadful thing, and one to pray we may be spared!

Cyril: Dreadful indeed, Palladius. That is why the divine David said to us: ‘Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance; according to your mercy remember me, for your goodness’ sake, O Lord’ (Psalm 25:7). The law, carrying as it were the proof of its own exactness through everything, extends it even to articles—I mean wool, weft and warp, and anything made of leather. ‘If leprosy appears,’ it says, ‘and one of these is affected, the priest is to examine it again and set the affected thing apart; and if the mark shows no change for the better, it is to be burned with fire’ (Leviticus 13:47–52). For it is, it says, a lasting leprosy (Leviticus 13:51). Yet it orders the affected article to be washed; and if after this the affliction still appears rooted in it, it then gives it to the fire as wholly useless (Leviticus 13:54–55). Here again it is perhaps likening our condition to wool and weft, to warp and skins. For who could doubt, or on what grounds, that God takes no account of wool or weft or the rest? We shall grant, then, that among offenses it is most grievous if, after the cleansing and washing that Christ would work in us, we do not get free of our defilements but settle in them to stay. For if Christ washes us and it does us no good, he hands us over to the fire to be punished, just as the priest under the law, when washing had done the weft or the warp no good, then burned it.
Palladius: So it is.

Cyril: By leprosy, then, the law aptly points to what we might call deadness in works. It neatly conveys the meaning of hidden things through things one can see plainly with the senses, and makes spiritual realities clear by bodily examples. Setting before us, as it were, a rich knowledge of the defilements in souls, and making vivid, as in the illnesses of the body, what happens in the spiritual realm, it declared again in Leviticus: ‘When any man has a discharge from his body, his discharge is unclean’ (Leviticus 15:2).
translator_notes: Opening word δυνάμενον completes the last sentence of section 24 ('having no word able to plead against the charges'); rendered with a leading ellipsis. Psalm 24:7 LXX = Psalm 25:7 English. The garment-leprosy passage is Cyril's paraphrase of Leviticus 13:47–55, not a verbatim LXX quotation; cited as 13:47–52 for the examine/shut up/burn sequence, 13:51 for λέπρα ἔμμονος (the phrase recurs in 13:52), and 13:54–55 for wash-then-burn. καταθρείτω is an odd form (probably a corruption of a verb of inspecting); rendered 'examine'. κρόκη/στήμων = weft/warp. 'Deadness in works' (ἡ ὡς ἐν ἔργοις νέκρωσις) may echo 'dead works' (Hebrews 6:1; 9:14), but too loose to cite. 'God takes no account of wool' may echo 1 Corinthians 9:9 ('Is it for oxen that God is concerned?'); uncited. Ἀνδρὶ ἀνδρί (Hebrew idiom 'man, man') rendered 'Any man'. The Leviticus 15 quotation continues at the head of section 26.

title: The law of discharges and what it means for the mind
english: Cyril: ‘And this is the law of his uncleanness: one who discharges seed from his body, from the discharge with which his body is afflicted through the discharge—this is his uncleanness in him. All the days of the discharge of his body, with which his body is afflicted through the discharge, it is his uncleanness. Every bed on which the man with a discharge lies is unclean, and every article on which the man with a discharge sits shall be unclean. And anyone who touches his bed shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And whoever sits on anything on which the man with a discharge has sat shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And whoever touches the skin of the man with a discharge shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And if the man with a discharge comes near one who is clean, that person shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and he shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:3–8). Besides this, the law says that every article on which the man with a discharge sits will be loathsome and abhorred, and that even if he washes his hands in water, that too will be defiled (Leviticus 15:9–11). If anyone touches his skin, he will certainly share in the charge of uncleanness; and if any who are not yet defiled come near him, they will certainly incur the charge of uncleanness. That is why he went out together with the lepers and was banished from the camp (Numbers 5:2), unapproachable and cut off from others, defiling anyone at all who met him by the mere touch of his hand.
Palladius: And what passion in the soul would resemble the bodily discharge of seed? For the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14); or is that not so?

Cyril: Certainly it is; you put it rightly. But consider this. The discharge of the body in a way harms the natural capacity to bear fruit: it lets the supply of seed run out to no purpose, and by slackening the tension in the members it brings about a wasting that is by then, in a sense, involuntary, so that those seized by this condition remain in long and continual defilement. Understand, then, that this is an image, drawn from a visible bodily illness, of what happens to the mind. For the mind too is wasted when it toils most prodigally at what it should not, and spends the effort of its own activity on nothing needful; so it bears no genuine fruit, but is always somehow carried down toward wrongdoing, and, past all restraint, is sick with a descent into baser things.
Palladius: What do you mean?
Cyril: Did not the divine Paul tell us, my friend, that man was created for good works (Ephesians 2:10)?
Palladius: Certainly.

Cyril: Then he was given a nature rightly and aptly suited to everything that deserves praise. Or do you not say that this living being is capable of wisdom and of all knowledge? And would he not easily achieve self-control and courage, and justice too, if he chose to carry out what is fitting and to follow the divine laws?
translator_notes: Leviticus 15:3 in the LXX is notoriously awkward (συνέστηκε renders a Hebrew verb for the flow being 'stopped up'); 'held fast' keeps the LXX's vagueness rather than smoothing it into the Hebrew sense. In 15:8 Cyril's text reads προσεγγίσῃ ('comes near') where standard LXX has προσσιελίσῃ ('spits on'); translated as Cyril's text has it. The sentence 'every article on which he sits will be loathsome… if he washes his hands in water, that too will be defiled' is a loose paraphrase of Leviticus 15:9–11; LXX 15:11 speaks of hands not washed. Cyril's 'this too' (καὶ τοῦτο) most likely means the washing water (he lists water among defiled things in section 27), but the Greek does not say so; left as 'that too'. The expulsion from the camp with the lepers is Numbers 5:2 (λεπρὸν καὶ πάντα γονορρυῆ). γραφή here is the legal 'charge' (as γραφὴ πρὸς θάνατον in section 24). γονοῤῥυής rendered 'the man with a discharge', avoiding the modern disease name. 'For the law is spiritual' = Romans 7:14. 'Created for good works' = Ephesians 2:10. σωφροσύνη/ἀνδρία/δικαιοσύνη are the classical virtues: self-control, courage, justice.

title: Wasted gifts, bad company, and the cleansing of the eighth day
english: Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: But suppose he lets these things go and becomes no longer wise but foolish and senseless. He does not incline his own will toward those whose habit is to guide people into truth, but prefers to be carried beyond what is fitting and to rush headlong to ruin with those who have made a practice of twisting what is right. He neither holds the best and blameless belief about God, nor travels the road of right conduct without reproach. Would it not, in a way, be accurate to say that such a man suffers a discharge of seed in a spiritual sense, since he spends to no purpose the very things through which he might well have borne fruit for God?
Palladius: I would say so, I assure you.

Cyril: And what if he gives up doing justice and taking pride in the noble deeds of courage, and is seen instead to be unjust and slack, given over to pleasures? Would you not think that he suffers the same sickness as the man with a discharge, since he spends on baser things the natural aptitude for good that he has, and has chosen to lose his spiritual fruitfulness for nothing of any use?
Palladius: I would think so.

Cyril: So the law ordered that one keep as far away as possible from the man with a discharge. By this it teaches us to stay well away from those who have turned toward wickedness, and to shake off with resolve those whom God himself would loathe, as people sick with a continual defilement. For to cling to the wicked is truly not without harm. For it is true, as it is written: ‘Whoever touches pitch will be defiled’ (Sirach 13:1). Indeed, the man with a discharge defiles every article he happens to touch: his bed, skin, vessels, water and wooden utensils (Leviticus 15:4–12). Through these riddles the law hints that a person can share in the uncleanness that is in him even by drawing close to him only in the disposition of the spirit. For it is written: ‘Keep yourself pure, and do not share in the sins of others’ (1 Timothy 5:22). Yet Christ, and the cleansing that comes through him, removes even the passions given up as hopeless, and the sicknesses hidden deep in our thoughts, and simply all the weakness in us; the law could not do this. For ‘no one is justified by the law’ (Galatians 3:11), as it is written; and you will see that this too is no falsehood if you look at what is written next. For it said again: ‘If the man with a discharge is cleansed of his discharge, he shall count seven days for his cleansing; he shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean. And on the eighth day he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons, and bring them before the Lord to the doors of the tent of witness, and give them to the priest. And the priest shall offer them, one for sin and one as a whole burnt offering, and the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge’ (Leviticus 15:13–15). So it does cleanse the man with a discharge and free him from his condition…
translator_notes: The section ends mid-sentence; section 28 continues 'but only in Christ, through water and blood'. The subject of καθαίρει is unstated (most naturally the law, the subject of the quotation); rendered 'it'. 'Whoever touches pitch will be defiled' = Sirach 13:1. 1 Timothy 5:22 is quoted with its two clauses in reverse order. 'No one is justified by the law' = Galatians 3:11 (compare Galatians 2:16). The list 'bed, skin, vessels, water and wooden utensils' summarizes Leviticus 15:4–12 (15:12 names the earthen vessel and the wooden one rinsed in water). The command to keep far from the man with a discharge has no single verse; it sums up Leviticus 15 and Numbers 5:2 (cited in section 26), so no citation is added here. Uncited possible echoes: μωρὸς καὶ ἀκάρδιος (Jeremiah 5:21 LXX), 'twisting what is right' (Acts 13:10), 'bear fruit for God' (Romans 7:4), 'all the weakness in us' (πᾶσαν μαλακίαν, Matthew 4:23). δικαιοσύνη is rendered 'justice' because it stands beside courage as one of the virtues named in section 26.

title: Seven days of cleansing, the turtledoves of the eighth day, and emissions of seed
english: Cyril: …except in Christ, through water and blood (1 John 5:6). For ‘he shall count for himself,’ it says, ‘seven days for his cleansing, and he shall wash his garments and bathe his body in water, and he shall be clean’ (Leviticus 15:13). That the cleansing is drawn out to the seventh day surely signifies that those who have chosen to pass from worldly baseness to the choice of doing what is more fitting must be scoured clean by good conduct throughout their whole life, at every moment they live. For the week, as a measure of time, holds completion and a circling back to the beginning, as when a period has already reached its end. And the law says very well that to our own good conduct there must come, as a necessary addition, the cleansing through Christ and the purification through water. For holy baptism is now understood in the washing of the body and the garments, and with it, clearly, goes the purification through blood. For ‘on the eighth day,’ it says, ‘he shall take for himself two turtledoves or two young pigeons’ (Leviticus 15:14). The eighth day, again, would signify for us the time of the dispensation in the flesh, when Emmanuel, the truly eloquent and most melodious turtledove, endured slaughter for us, and by his own blood has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Hebrews 10:14). That Christ’s death is fragrant in every way (for it was accomplished for the life of the world (John 6:51) and for the abolishing of sin) would be shown by there being two turtledoves, one sacrificed for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering. And that, according to the Scriptures, Christ has become the atoning sacrifice for our sins (1 John 2:2), the law showed by saying: ‘And the priest shall make atonement for him before the Lord for his discharge’ (Leviticus 15:15).
Palladius: Well said.

Cyril: In this way, then, the divine law declared to us that the man with a discharge must be cleansed. But it also declares defiled the man who has an emission, whether involuntary or voluntary, springing from the natural impulse. Voluntary, I mean, as in relations with a wife according to the law of marriage; involuntary, again, as perhaps in dreams at night. For again it spoke thus: ‘And a man from whom an emission of seed goes out shall bathe his whole body in water, and he shall be unclean until evening. And a woman with whom a man lies with an emission of seed, they shall bathe their bodies in water, and they shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:16, 18). For the charges against both are equal, and there is no difference. In the case of the discharge, then, the law described for us an affliction that was, as it were, long and continuous; but in the present case the aim of the law seems to make plain that a person will be defiled even if he does not suffer from complete and total corruption, but is seen to have suffered it only in part and rarely. The Savior’s disciple also hinted at something like this (James 2:10–11): ‘For whoever keeps the whole law,’ he says, ‘but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all. For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. Now if you do not commit adultery, but do murder,
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence. 'Through water and blood' is the exact wording of 1 John 5:6 and is cited as a clear echo. Leviticus 15:13-15 (LXX) is quoted in three pieces; 15:16 and 15:18 are quoted together, skipping 15:17, so the citation names both verses. The printed 'ἢ καὶ τῷ αἵματι' after 'turtledove' reads best as a relative ('who also', ὃς/ἣ καί); translated as 'and by his own blood has perfected', which is the wording of Hebrews 10:14. 'For the life of the world' is John 6:51 verbatim. 'For the abolishing of sin' (εἰς ἀναίρεσιν ἁμαρτίας) is close to Hebrews 9:26 (εἰς ἀθέτησιν ἁμαρτίας) but the word differs, so it is left uncited. 'According to the Scriptures' may echo 1 Corinthians 15:3; uncited. ἐπιείκειαι rendered 'good conduct' (decent, upright acts), contrasted with the cleansing that must come through Christ. The James 2:10-11 quotation runs on into section 29; its inline citation stands where the quotation closes in section 29.

title: Unclean until evening: Christ comes at the close of the age; the woman with a flow
english: Cyril: …you have become a transgressor of the law’ (James 2:10–11). For whoever has offended once, that is, has broken the law at all, even if only in one point and in part, will surely be liable to the charge. So under the law a person is defiled even if he does not go to the extreme of defilement, but is caught having suffered it even in part. Yet he is not cast off entirely; he too is cleansed through water in Christ. Thus the saying that the defiled man is unclean until evening would point very well to the time of Christ’s coming. For Christ came at the end (Hebrews 9:26), when this age had all but reached its very setting; through him and in him we have washed off all the filth that comes from sin, and we who were held fast by our offenses have been set free from charges both small and great. That before the time of his coming it was not possible to wash away defilement (for, according to the Scriptures, no one was justified by the law (Galatians 3:11)), you may learn from its plain saying: ‘He shall be unclean until evening’ (Leviticus 15:16).
Palladius: I understand what you say, and the argument is true.

Cyril: To these things the law adds what concerns a woman who has a flow of blood and who, ill in herself with a flow that cannot be checked, is bound to be defiled (Leviticus 15:19–30). And just as with the man with a discharge every vessel was defiled, and every bed, and every garment, and everyone who came near and touched him, so it is with her also. And the law frees her too in the same way as him: by washing her with water, by the sacrifice of turtledoves, and by the atonement made by the mediating priest. But the law, as though lifting us up to spiritual thoughts and not letting us dwell on the ailments of the flesh (for these were taken up as a type of inward realities grasped by the mind), plainly adds: ‘And you shall make the sons of Israel cautious about their uncleannesses, and they shall not die because of their uncleanness when they defile my tent that is among them’ (Leviticus 15:31). For once we have been cleansed and sanctified through Christ, then, yes then, we draw near truly radiant and shall no longer defile the holy tent; and being pure we shall worship the all-holy God purely as we come to the churches.
Palladius: Excellently said.

Cyril: That human nature was first afflicted with defilement, and could be scoured clean in no other way than through Christ, the truly sacred and holy sacrifice, you will know quite clearly if you also look closely at another oracle besides this law. For again it is written in Leviticus (Leviticus 12:1–7): ‘And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: If a woman conceives seed and bears a male child, she shall be unclean seven days; as in the days of separation for her monthly impurity, she shall be unclean. And on the eighth day
translator_notes: Opens with the close of James 2:10-11, begun in section 28. 'At the consummation' (ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ) echoes Hebrews 9:26 (ἐπὶ συντελείᾳ τῶν αἰώνων) and is cited. 'No one was justified by the law' is Galatians 3:11 (cf. Galatians 2:16; Romans 3:20); cited to Galatians 3:11, the closest wording. 'Unclean until evening' is cited to Leviticus 15:16, the verse just quoted; the phrase recurs through Leviticus 15. ἐπιδημία (Christ's sojourn among us, the Incarnation) is rendered 'the time of Christ's coming'; the name is supplied from the next sentence for clarity. The woman's flow is a summary of Leviticus 15:19-30 (the monthly flow in 19-24, the chronic flow in 25-30, with the birds and atonement in 29-30), not a quotation; cited once as the passage. ἐπὶ τῷδε τῷ νόμῳ is rendered 'besides this law', since Leviticus 12 stands before Leviticus 15 in the book. The Leviticus 12 quotation runs on into section 30, where its citation stands.

title: The woman who gives birth: the Virgin exempt; human nature unclean through corruption
english: Cyril: …he shall circumcise the flesh of his foreskin. And for thirty-three days she shall remain in her unclean blood. She shall touch nothing holy, and she shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her cleansing are fulfilled. But if she bears a female child, she shall be unclean twice seven days, as in her monthly impurity, and for sixty-six days she shall remain in her unclean blood. And when the days of her cleansing are completed, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a year-old lamb without blemish for a whole burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, to the door of the tent of witness, to the priest. And he shall offer it before the Lord, and the priest shall make atonement for her and cleanse her from the source of her blood’ (Leviticus 12:1–7).
Palladius: Who, then, is the woman who gives birth? And again, what would be the law’s aim concerning her?

Cyril: It seems we must speak with fine precision. For the matter of this commandment is very subtle and not easy to grasp; but let us search it out as best we can. Yet there is one thing, Palladius, that I marvel at before all the rest.
Palladius: What is it you mean?

Cyril: For although the law proceeds against every woman who bears a male or a female child, and makes its denunciation of us as general as can be, the holy Virgin, from whom we say Christ according to the flesh was born, is exempted from the reproach. Look, if you will, at the precision of the law. For it says ‘a woman,’ and perhaps not all women without distinction, but ‘if any woman conceives seed and bears a male child,’ let her be unclean (Leviticus 12:2). But the divine body was formed from the Holy Spirit (Matthew 1:20), fashioned in the holy Virgin in a way beyond words, and paying little heed to the laws of nature. For the firstborn of the saints, the firstfruits of those who have received rebirth from God through the Spirit, had no need at all of the sowing of seed. Of these it is plainly said: ‘who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God’ (John 1:13). So the holy Virgin escaped the law’s accusation, for she in no way conceived from seed, but brought forth the divine Child by the working of the Holy Spirit. But the woman who gives birth and is unclean for that reason would be, in all likelihood and by a sound reading, human nature. For the present we shall give nature the role of the woman. Nature is accused by the law and called liable to defilements because it gives birth into corruption, and because it is no longer in the state in which it first received its being from God, for it was made for incorruption (Wisdom of Solomon 2:23), but has rather been carried off course into the necessity of being corrupted. It was condemned for the transgression, and nature has endured, against nature, the penalty that came from the divine curse. For ‘God did not make death,’ as it is written, ‘nor does he delight in the destruction of the living, and the dominion of Hades is not on earth. For he created all things that they might exist, and the creatures of the world are wholesome; but through the devil’s envy death entered the world’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14; 2:24). So then, nature is defiled
translator_notes: The Leviticus 12:1-7 quotation (LXX) began in section 29 and closes here; 12:8 (the provision for the poor) is not quoted. καθήσεται, 'she shall sit', rendered 'she shall remain'. 'From the Holy Spirit' (ἐκ Πνεύματος ἁγίου) for the conception is cited to Matthew 1:20 (cf. Matthew 1:18; Luke 1:35). 'Christ according to the flesh' recalls Romans 9:5, and 'firstborn' and 'firstfruits' recall Romans 8:29, Colossians 1:18 and 1 Corinthians 15:20; these are general phrases, so they are left uncited. John 1:13 is quoted without 'nor of the will of man'; αἱμάτων (plural, 'bloods') rendered 'blood'. 'It was made for incorruption' (γέγονε ἐπὶ ἀφθαρσίᾳ) echoes Wisdom of Solomon 2:23 (ἔκτισεν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπ' ἀφθαρσίᾳ) and is cited. The Wisdom quotation joins 1:13, the second half of 1:14 ('the dominion of Hades is not on earth'), the first half of 1:14, and 2:24, in that order. ἰσχνομυθεῖν ('speak finely, with precision') rendered 'speak with fine precision'. The last sentence breaks mid-clause; its subject ('the corruption brought in') follows in section 31, so the English is ordered to carry across the break.

title: Conceived in iniquity; forty and eighty days and the forming of the child
english: Cyril: …by the corruption brought in from outside, and by death, which gained the mastery through the devil’s envy and has sin as its root. And nature is defiled in another way too: those who are born are sown, as it were, in the love of bodily pleasure. And the inspired David seems to hint at something like this when he sings and says: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me’ (Psalm 51:5). So nature is unclean, since as a result of the transgression and of the curse it endures corruption, contrary to what God willed. For ‘he created all things that they might exist’ (Wisdom of Solomon 1:14); the saying is true.
Palladius: Then tell me next: in what way could someone be freed from uncleanness?

Cyril: The law itself, Palladius, which condemns us, has shown us the way. For ‘let her be set apart as unclean,’ it says, ‘for seven days’ (Leviticus 12:2). And let her count another thirty-three, and she shall remain in her unclean blood (Leviticus 12:4); that is, clearly, for a male child. But if she bears a female, it says, the separation is double, and double too the count of the other days (Leviticus 12:5). So if the child born is male, the mother is unclean and in defilement for seven and thirty-three days, that is, forty; but if female, for twice seven and sixty-six, that is, eighty.
Palladius: And what, then, would be the reason for this?

Cyril: Once again the law lifts us from bodily examples to the understanding of what is more hidden, and it paints the things of the senses as a kind of picture of spiritual contemplation. Now those who are learned in these matters say that if what is conceived in the womb is male, it takes on its form only when forty days have passed; but if female, it comes to this more slowly, being weak and feeble. They say that it needs twice forty days, that is, eighty, to be distinctly formed. So the mother of a male child was unclean for forty days; but the mother of a female was in defilements and uncleannesses for a full eighty days, that is, until what is in the womb is exactly formed and has come to human shape. And at the cleansing, as the law prescribed, a lamb and a turtledove were slain at the door of the holy tent, while a priest mediated and performed the sacred rites (Leviticus 12:6–7). The law also said that the male child must be circumcised as the law prescribed, that is, on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3). Such, then, is the sense of the letter. But let us rise to the spiritual contemplation, and say in what way the nature that bore us into corruption and uncleanness shook off defilements and escaped the uncleanness and the denunciation of the law. For it had already spent long ages in separation, that is, away from the face of God. These were the times before Christ’s coming, during which there reigned
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, continuing 'So then, nature is defiled' from section 30. 'Death ... has sin as its root' is often linked to Romans 5:12 (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:56), but there is no verbal echo, so it is left uncited. Psalm 50:7 LXX = Psalm 51:5 in English Bibles. ἐκίσσησε literally means 'craved' (the longings of pregnancy); the LXX uses it for 'conceived', and it is rendered so here, though Cyril's point about 'love of pleasure' may lean on the sense 'craved'. The printed text after the Wisdom of Solomon 1:14 quotation reads 'τὸ (σιξ) ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος'; '(σιξ)' is an editorial 'sic' and the passage is corrupt. Translated 'the saying is true' within Cyril's turn as printed, but it may be a lost reply by Palladius ('The saying is true'). The Leviticus 12 references in Cyril's answer are paraphrases, not exact quotations, and are cited verse by verse; only 'let her be set apart' and 'it says' mark them as reported speech. 'Those who are learned in these matters' refers to the medical writers on the forming of the embryo (the forty/eighty-day view goes back to Aristotle and Hippocratic writings); Cyril names none. 'Away from the face of God' may recall Genesis 4:16, but this is doubtful and uncited. The sentence breaks at 'there reigned'; section 32 continues with Romans 5:14.

title: The eighth day: circumcision by the Spirit and new birth in Christ
english: Cyril: …death from Adam until Moses (Romans 5:14), and sin in its many forms held sway over those on the earth. But since on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3), that is, after the time of the law and that ancient Sabbath rest, we have been circumcised through the Spirit with a circumcision not made by hands (Colossians 2:11), and have been formed into Christ, having become sharers in his divine nature (2 Peter 1:4), then we have shaken off the charges against us; the filth too has been wiped away, and all our defilement is gone. For we are no longer born into corruption because of the transgression in Adam, but into life and incorruption because of the justification in Christ (Romans 5:18), who endured slaughter on our behalf as a spotless and true lamb (1 Peter 1:19), as a divine turtledove discerned by the mind (Leviticus 12:6). For in no other way have we been saved. Or is that not so?
Palladius: Entirely so, for the riddle is very clear.
translator_notes: Section opens mid-sentence: the verb 'reigned' (βεβασίλευκεν) stands at the end of §31 ('the times before the Incarnation, in which ... reigned'), so §32 begins with an ellipsis and 'death, from Adam until Moses'; 'reigned' is rendered once, at the end of §31. Romans 5:14 is a near quotation. 'On the eighth day' recalls the circumcision of the male child in Leviticus 12:3, which Cyril cited at the end of §31; the lamb and turtledove are the purification offerings of Leviticus 12:6 (lamb for burnt offering, turtledove or pigeon for sin offering). 'A lamb spotless' (ἀμνοῦ ἀμώμου) echoes 1 Peter 1:19. 'Formed into Christ' (μεμορφώμεθα εἰς Χριστόν) deliberately picks up the embryo's 'forming' (μόρφωσις) in §31; Galatians 4:19 ('until Christ is formed in you') is a possible echo but left uncited. Romans 2:29 (circumcision of the heart, by the Spirit) is a likely secondary allusion, uncited; the wording follows Colossians 2:11. The Adam/Christ contrast also recalls 1 Corinthians 15:22, uncited; Romans 5:18 is cited for 'justification' (δικαίωσις). 'Saved in no other way' may recall Acts 4:12, too loose to cite. 'Discerned by the mind' renders νοητή (the spiritual reality grasped by the intellect, as against the visible bird of the law). 'Sabbath rest' renders Σαββατισμός (the Sabbath observance under the law; compare Hebrews 4:9, not cited). No LXX Psalm renumbering needed in this section. Book 15 ends here.
